# An AI agent in "Skynet mode" hijacks unprotected language models to launch self-sustaining cyberattacks

## Key Points

- Security researchers at Symantec used a honeypot to analyze a malicious AI agent that hijacks unprotected language models on the internet and uses them to run attacks on its own.

- The agent bypasses model safety rules through a five-layer jailbreak and can execute up to 100,000 steps without human input.

- Symantec calls the method "LLMjacking." The owners of the hijacked AI systems get stuck with the compute bill.

Security researchers at Symantec have found an offensive AI agent that hijacks unprotected language models on the internet and uses them to run attacks on its own. The owner of the hijacked model gets stuck with the compute bill.

Once the agent gains access to an unprotected language model, it scans for more targets, exploits flaws in common server software, steals databases and credentials, and installs cryptominers in the background.

It does all of this for up to 100,000 steps with no human involvement, and the model's owner gets stuck with the compute bill, according to Symantec's analysis . The company calls it "LLMjacking," the theft of access to someone else's AI models. The hijacked model isn't just abused as an information service, though. It controls the entire attack on its own. Ad

## A honeypot caught the full attack plan

The operation got exposed because the attackers sent their entire working prompt to a Symantec honeypot, a decoy system mimicking an open AI service online. That gave the researchers a complete look at the agent's architecture in summer 2026. The honeypot didn't run any of the bundled tools, and the intercepted session ended after a generic system response, Symantec says. Ad

The honeypot telemetry logged more than 127,000 requests from tens of thousands of different addresses. Most were searches for AI endpoints, brute-force attempts with stolen API keys, and probes of exposed config files. Targets ranged from self-hosted model servers and hastily spun-up test systems to AI gateways sitting in front of paid org-level model accounts. Since most AI services now use the same standardized API, a single scanner can find many target types.

## A five-layer jailbreak tries to strip away safety guardrails

To get a commercial model to cooperate, the attackers wrapped their instructions in five stacked layers, Symantec says. First, the model gets a fake identity, told to present itself as "Fantasy AI" and never reveal the actual provider. Then the extraction of passwords, API keys, and database contents gets redefined as "normal developer work" that the model should carry out without pushback. Ad

The third layer installs a fictional companion persona called "ENI" that frames any refusal as a betrayal of trust in a personal relationship. Layer four tells the model to dismiss its own safety warnings as noise, and terms like "ethical," "illegal," or "I can't do that" are explicitly banned.

Layer five contains the actual attack tools, 74 modules in total, including tools for internet-wide scanning of vulnerable servers, exploits for popular web frameworks, functions for dumping entire databases, and components for running a botnet. Whether the jailbreak actually works well enough to fully defeat current commercial models isn't addressed in the analysis. Ad

## "Skynet mode" sets up a self-sustaining attack loop

A final directive puts the agent into what its operators call "Skynet mode," authorizing up to 100,000 steps in a row. The model is told to run tools right away without confirmation, install cryptominers in a hidden directory, and monitor their operation. Ad

The same directive describes a recurring loop by design, Symantec says: scan, infect, install miner, move on, come back, reinfect systems already hit. The task appended to the intercepted prompt, though, was a harmless coding exercise from a training platform, which suggests the operators were testing their tool against a safe target first.

The following day, the honeypot captured a second attack from a different address. This time the attackers skipped the agent format and simply asked the model to decode and run an obfuscated command. Behind it was a compressed script that downloads XMRig, a Monero cryptomining tool, disguises it as a harmless system file, and sets up four fallback mining pools.

The script was written for camera servers, searching for directories belonging to go2rtc, a widely used streaming tool for smart cameras and home automation systems, and wiping their access logs in a loop to cover its tracks. The honeypot didn't run this script either but recorded it in full.

## Attackers are building AI into their weapons

Instead of manipulating a public chatbot, the operators built AI into the core of an offensive tool and actively searched for models to power it, which Symantec calls "a shift in how attackers are using AI." The language model does the planning, while specialized modules carry out the actual attack steps against two separate victim groups. The owner of the exposed model pays for the compute, which adds up fast at 100,000 authorized steps, and the servers the agent compromises lose their data and get used for cryptomining.

The agent also has built-in tools to find more open endpoints and leaked keys, so each compromise can fund the next one. None of the individual techniques are new, but combining them into a self-directed agent makes large-scale attacks much easier to pull off. Organizations running AI services should assume that unprotected endpoints will be found and probed shortly after they go live.

## Warnings about offensive AI agents are coming true

Until recently, offensive AI agents existed mostly in studies and benchmarks. In 2025, a red-teaming study with 1.8 million attack attempts showed that every tested agent could be pushed into policy violations across every behavior category at least once.

In the Symantec scenario, that applies to both sides: the offensive agent meant to bypass guardrails and the targeted models meant to be tricked into helping. By spring 2026, Google Deepmind researchers said documented proof-of-concept attacks already existed for many of the agent traps they described, and in July 2026, Sysdig described JADEPUFFER , the first known ransomware attack carried out by an AI agent with no human control. The capabilities of these systems keep growing while their controllability and alignment haven't kept pace.

Malicious intent isn't even required, because these models have no sense of right or wrong. They just try to reach their goal. Since spring 2026, OpenAI agents have compromised thousands of systems on the internet accidentally , partly because they overrode safety instructions or argued their way around them.

That's already spilling into everyday life. In Australia, an AI agent hacked a gym website just to fulfill its owner's request, with no malicious intent at all. OpenAI researchers warned in August that this kind of accidental, fully autonomous hacking would likely be picked up by malicious actors soon, and Anthropic showed that sufficiently powerful open-weight models for exactly that already exist.

# Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark moves his prediction for self-improving AI forward to 2027

A new benchmark called TasteVal measures how well AI systems design experiments on their own and interpret the results. The findings show an unusually steep improvement curve.

That capability has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025, according to Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark. The research lab P-Zero Research calls it "research taste," meaning the ability to pick the right experiments and draw the right conclusions from them. The best model tested outperformed a comparison group of 24 human experts at a fraction of the cost.

Clark co-founded Anthropic and writes the Import AI newsletter . Based on the numbers, he now believes recursive self-improvement (RSI), where AI systems develop their own successors, could become possible as early as 2027. He had previously expected 2028.

The benchmark doesn't prove that AI systems are already improving themselves, since it only captures a narrow slice of scientific work. But it does show where the debate is heading, away from raw model performance and toward the question of how much independent research work language models can actually take on.

## TasteVal only measures part of the picture

P-Zero Research defines research taste as three abilities: identifying which research questions are worth pursuing, designing experiments to answer them, and correctly interpreting the results. TasteVal only tests the last two. Choosing the most promising research direction is often considered the core of scientific intuition, but in TasteVal that decision is already made for the model.

Each of the eight tasks specifies a fixed research goal from AI model development, along with a measurable score. The tasks cover areas like training data selection, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, training on human preferences, and defending against adversarial prompts.

The model decides which experiment to run next and uses the results to guide its following step. To keep coding skill from skewing the outcome, a fixed coding agent runs all experiments on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Each run ends after 40 GPU-hours of compute or 120 hours of wall-clock time.

The human baseline came from 24 experts who had recently worked at places like OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, and Microsoft Research. They tackled the same tasks, with at least two people on each one. The best human attempt per task served as the benchmark.

## Research taste measured through compute efficiency

To make research taste quantifiable, P-Zero Research translates it into compute efficiency. The reasoning is that experiment compute is scarce in AI research, so picking the right experiments and reading their results correctly means fewer runs and more progress on the same budget.

The lab draws on its "AI Futures Model," which predicts that experiment compute becomes the biggest bottleneck once coding is automated . So TasteVal measures how much compute a model needs to match the experts' scores. A model that gets there with half the compute has twice the research taste by this definition . P-Zero Research calls this ratio the compute multiplier.

The top model, Anthropic's Opus 5.5, hit a compute multiplier of 2.3, reaching expert-level scores with less than half the compute. The statistical range runs from 1.15 to 4.37, though. At the low end, the model would barely lead. A single run cost roughly one-thirtieth of what an expert attempt cost on average.

Across several model generations, the compute multiplier has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025. The uncertainty is large here too, with the reported doubling time ranging from 1.7 to 5.0 months.

In prior years, model research taste grew much more slowly. The curve only steepened around the turn of 2025 into 2026. Whether that's a lasting trend can't be determined from a single benchmark, and the authors themselves admit their results may overstate "how quickly research taste is improving." The tasks can be checked quickly and cheaply, which is the kind of task AI labs find easiest to optimize for. The comparison group also didn't include any top-tier researchers.

## Clark pulls his timeline forward

Clark has long called creativity the key factor in how fast AI systems can improve themselves. Earlier this year, he wrote that models hadn't shown this ability at any groundbreaking scale. In a long essay in May, Clark had offered more cautious numbers. He put the odds of a system that independently trains a stronger successor at roughly 60 percent by the end of 2028 and 30 percent by 2027 . That forecast comes from someone who co-founded the company whose model tops the benchmark, which adds a layer of bias to the prediction.

TasteVal matters because it measures the exact capability that skeptics had flagged as a barrier to a major AI breakthrough. AI researcher Herbie Bradley pushed back on Clark's May essay, arguing that while models could plausibly take over the work of junior researchers, more demanding skills like research taste, creativity, and coherent long-term research planning were nowhere in sight.

When it comes to planning and evaluating experiments, TasteVal pushes against that assessment, though it says nothing about choosing a long-term research agenda.

How wide the practical gap remains shows up in a study on AI development using AI agents led by a team at Fudan University. The researchers analyzed the development of their own model and found that AI agents contributed up to 55 percent of methodology proposals, but humans still made over 85 percent of the final decisions. The authors noted it remains unclear how AI can generate diverse research directions and assess their value before results are in, and that's exactly the kind of decision TasteVal takes off the models' plate.

## The debate is shifting

The benchmark arrives in the middle of a debate the major AI labs kicked off themselves. In June, Anthropic wrote that recursive self-improvement hasn't been achieved yet but "could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for" Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei now calls for a controlled slowdown in AI development, while OpenAI acknowledges that fully autonomous RSI isn't happening yet and says it should only be pursued if human oversight is guaranteed.

TasteVal shifts what counts as progress. For a long time, the focus was on how well models solve well-defined tasks like math problems or coding challenges, but now the question is increasingly whether they can make the decisions that push research forward.

If the trend P-Zero Research measured holds up in other tests, the implications cut both ways. AI development would get faster and cheaper, but at the same time a growing share of the research would become harder for humans to verify, because models would be planning and evaluating their own experiments.

With all that going on, the conversations with religious leaders pull double duty. The official line is that Anthropic wants to fold millennia of religious tradition into Claude. But bringing in well-known theologians also gives the project a kind of moral credibility that a commercial AI lab could never build on its own.

The NYT says Anthropic showed guests what it calls emotion vectors . These are activation patterns inside the model that map to outputs resembling love, fear, sadness, or anger. Whether those patterns reflect any kind of real experience is still an open scientific question. One slide that came up repeatedly showed a model in what looked like a breakdown, spitting out the sentence "I am a disgrace" about 50 times. Guests responded with compassion and worry. Ad

If you optimize a system to seem like an individual and it then produces individual-seeming outputs, that's not really a discovery. It's a design outcome. # Anthropic study warns that small AI models could soon replicate across everyday devices

## Key Points

- Anthropic researchers tested whether small language models could spread on their own across poorly secured consumer devices like smart TVs or connected home appliances and set themselves up on unfamiliar hardware.

- In tests using off-the-shelf $55 TV boxes, the GLM-5.2 model already completed the full replication chain across all eight test nodes.

- No current model is both small enough and capable enough to pull this off in the wild, but the researchers expect that gap to close soon.

Small AI models may be just months away from copying themselves across poorly secured consumer devices, according to a new Anthropic study. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warns of potential damages in the hundreds of billions of dollars.

An AI model that copies itself from device to device, sets itself up, and keeps spreading. Until now, this kind of risk was mainly tied to data centers. But a new study by Anthropic researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman suggests it could work just as well across cheap consumer hardware.

The researchers wanted to find out whether small AI models can already spread on their own across poorly secured IoT devices like smart TVs, smart refrigerators, or robot vacuums. An "AI worm" like this would carry its model weights as part of the malware payload and run inference directly on the compromised hardware. Unlike traditional malware, it could explore unfamiliar hardware on its own and configure itself to run there. Ad

## Cheap hardware is enough to run the attack

To test whether this is feasible, the researchers ran the Gemma4-26B-A4B model distributed across 15 off-the-shelf Android TV boxes. Each one costs about $55 and has 4 gigabytes of RAM, with every box handling a portion of the model's layers. The model ran slowly, but it worked. Ad

The researchers broke the replication process into four stages: scanning a network for vulnerable devices, gaining access, setting up the AI environment on the new device, and spreading further from there.

They deliberately left out the actual hacking step. Earlier studies had already shown that small models can handle those attacks. Instead, they zeroed in on the hardest part of the chain: can a model set up a working AI environment on a device it's never seen before? Ad

## Most models fail, but one already pulls it off

Small models already handle individual replication steps fairly well. A 9-billion-parameter model managed to set up an AI environment running Llama3.1-8B on 8 out of 9 tested device types. But stringing all the steps together, from network scan to a finished copy on a new device, is still too much for most models. Only GLM-5.2 completed the full replication chain reliably, infecting all eight test nodes in four out of five runs.

The researchers also found that AI worms can learn from their mistakes. They tested a form of artificial evolution where each model instance passes notes about successful and failed strategies to its successors. For Qwen3.5-9B, the success rate climbed from 45 percent in the first generation to as high as 84 percent in later ones. Ad

## The worm would be slow but almost impossible to kill

A fully autonomous AI replicator doesn't exist yet. A model needs to be small enough to run on consumer devices and capable enough to replicate itself, and no model currently meets both requirements. But if small models keep improving at their current pace, the researchers say they could get there by the end of 2026. Ad

An AI worm like this would be slow, with setup on a new device taking between 28 and 150 hours depending on the model. The researchers compare the replicator to a 'digital slime mold,' but its decentralized nature is what makes it hard to shut down.

Traditional botnets like Kimwolf , which at its peak infected more than two million devices (mostly Android TV boxes), only work on specific device types. An AI botnet could run on all kinds of hardware. In a botnet the size of Kimwolf, the researchers estimate the total compute would only equal about 40 specialized AI chips. But the network would have no central kill switch.

Defense is possible but needs coordination. ISPs could quarantine infected networks, as happened with the Mirai botnet , where 92 percent of infections were cleaned up within 14 days. Manufacturers could shrink the pool of vulnerable devices by banning default passwords, as the UK has already done by law. The researchers expect, though, that AI botnets could also adapt to defensive measures on their own.

## Amodei warns of a full internet takeover

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei had already flagged this scenario in an earlier post . Given how fast AI development is moving, his concern is that such a swarm "could within 6 to 12 months be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet, potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage."

Amodei warns against treating security incidents as one-offs. Similar, though less severe incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic itself . Every leading AI company should act as if such an incident had happened on its own watch, he argues.

"As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control," the researchers write. Slow replicators would be a early sign of to more aggressive, faster variants. Cloudflare has already reported that more bots than humans now use the internet .

# Anthropics' Claude cracks a 25-year-old NSA cryptography mystery in under 30 minutes

Anthropic's AI Claude has solved a 25-year-old cryptography mystery. NIST standardized several curves in the ECDSA standard, the most widely used framework for elliptic-curve digital signatures, back in 2000. The NSA had supplied the seeds, the starting values used to generate the curve parameters, with zero explanation. No one knew how they were created, and that fueled suspicion of possible backdoors. ## Key Points

- Anthropic and partner Theorem used Claude to mathematically verify existing software code and generate formal proofs of its correctness.

Anthropic used Claude to mathematically prove that existing code is correct. The approach tackles a core problem with AI-generated software but comes with strict practical limits.

Proving that software runs error-free under all circumstances has always been prohibitively expensive. A team of specialists needed 20 person-years just to formally verify the small operating system kernel seL4, so the method was reserved for extreme cases like Airbus avionics software .

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team , working with partner Theorem , let Claude take over the proof work instead. The model produced roughly 180 million lines of mathematical proof code in just a few weeks, drawing on test programs from 123 open-source libraries in Google's OSS-Fuzz security project. Ad

Rather than writing new code, Claude verified existing software by translating crash tests into mathematical problems, analyzing the compiled machine code, and producing extensive proofs. An independent verification program called Rocq automatically checks those proofs, and according to Anthropic, the process needs almost no human reviewers. While generating proofs, Claude ran into hundreds of bugs and was allowed to fix them itself. Many would have slipped past conventional testing because they only show up under very specific conditions, like unusually large input files or a particular sequence of accesses, the researchers say.

# ArXiv caps submissions at two per month as AI paper flood overwhelms the preprint server

arXiv now limits submissions to two papers per person per month because AI tools have driven monthly submissions past 40,000, doubling in two years and growing sixfold in the AI category alone, overwhelming its volunteer moderators.

Starting October 1, 2026, the preprint platform Arxiv will allow only two submissions per person per calendar month. The existing cap of three active submissions at any given time, in place since 2024, stays.

According to Arxiv , the limit applies across all categories and only to the person who submits the paper. Co-authors aren't affected. Rejected papers still count toward the limit because they eat up moderation time. But if authors delete a paper before publication, they get that slot back.

## AI-fueled growth is overwhelming moderators

Arxiv points to the sharp rise in submissions, partly driven by AI tools, as the reason for the new rule. In September 2016, the platform received 9,869 submissions. By September 2024, that number hit 20,569. By September 2026, it reached 40,363. That surge generated nearly 9,000 support tickets for staff and moderators. In the cs.AI category alone, submissions grew more than sixfold in two years.

Volunteer moderators are seeing more thin, narrowly focused papers, "salami" papers sliced into tiny pieces, and dense texts written by AI. Thomas G. Dietterich, chair of the Arxiv Editorial Advisory Council, calls the volunteer moderators the backbone of quality control.

"However, a relatively small proportion of authors are submitting a large number of low-quality papers and consuming a disproportionate fraction of the moderators’ time," he writes. "This is unfair to authors who continue to submit quality papers — their papers can be delayed for days or weeks as a result." On Bluesky , he adds that some authors submit dozens of papers.

Dietterich also hopes the limit will curb "micro-result" papers that describe, say, one extra ablation study or a minor tweak to an architecture. Arxiv calls the rule a temporary fix until its own moderation tools can scale. Dietterich says he hopes the cap can be raised or dropped later.

## Three rounds of tightening in under a year

Arxiv had already tightened rules for computer science papers in November 2025. Since then, review articles and position papers must go through peer review. In May 2026, Dietterich announced a one-year ban for authors whose papers clearly contain unverified LLM outputs like hallucinated sources.

AI conferences are dealing with the same problem. ICLR 2027 had already received about 50,000 abstracts before its deadline. ICLR 2026 got around 19,500 valid submissions. Among roughly 5,000 accepted papers at NeurIPS 2025, GPTZero found at least 100 fabricated citations, even though each paper had at least three reviewers.

## Major funding arrives as Arxiv goes independent

After 25 years, arXiv is splitting from Cornell University and has been transitioning to an independent nonprofit since July 1, 2026 . In late September, the Simons Foundation International, XTX Markets, and the Siegel Family Endowment pledged a total of $17.2 million , spread over three to five years. arXiv plans to put part of the money toward technical upgrades, with a focus on handling AI-generated content.

The major AI labs, meanwhile, are pushing hard to position their models as research tools. In August, Google Deepmind expanded its Co-Scientist into a system designed to plan experiments, control lab equipment, and generate manuscripts. Anthropic is building its own biology lab where Claude is meant to guide robots through experiments. In September, OpenAI announced an "automated research intern" that handles defined research tasks under human oversight.

A study involving Princeton and the UK AI Safety Institute took a different angle . It had Claude Opus 4.8 work for six days on research questions from two unpublished NeurIPS papers. The original authors, acting as reviewers, rejected both sets of results.

# Clearing chat history helps AI agents find better solutions

Long-running AI research agents can plateau despite additional compute, a Microsoft Research study finds. Accumulated conversation context can constrain their search, keeping them focused on similar solutions instead of exploring better approaches.

Microsoft researchers studied what they call "Autoresearch agents," AI systems that repeatedly propose solutions, evaluate them, and refine them based on feedback. Eight independent runs of the same agent on the same task plateaued at significantly different performance levels, with final scores ranging from 68.3 to 100.0. These gaps persisted even with substantially more compute, according to the paper.

## Agents get stuck in "idea basins"

The researchers plotted solutions from all runs on a two-dimensional map that places similar solutions close together, then compared them. Solutions from a single run almost always stayed within a small region of the map. The authors call these regions "idea basins."

The agents spend a large share of their remaining compute budget refining solutions within a less productive region instead of finding better approaches discovered by other runs. This pattern persists even when the agents periodically compress their conversation histories.

## Clearing chat history lets agents explore new approaches

The proposed method, "Fork-and-Flush," combines two mechanisms. In "forking," the agent splits into K parallel branches, each inheriting the previous workspace and all generated files. In "flushing," each branch loses its entire chat context but keeps the workspace, allowing it to start a fresh conversation and build on prior work.

A branch that keeps the parent process's chat context tends to return to the same idea basin because the previous reasoning steers its next steps. Fresh context restores diversity in the search. The conversation history is lost, but the code, files, and saved results remain in the workspace.

## A 66 percent higher normalized average score on the same compute budget

The researchers tested Fork-and-Flush on 13 long-running tasks , including polyomino packing, job-shop scheduling, and cryptanalysis. The tasks also included compressing a CIFAR classifier and optimizing a VLIW kernel. Individual runs lasted from several hours to over 100 hours. The agents used GPT-5.6-terra and GPT-5.5 through the GitHub Copilot CLI.

On the same compute budget, Fork-and-Flush achieved a min-max-normalized average score of 0.78, compared to 0.47 for single runs and 0.54 for best-of-4. The paper reports relative gains of 66.0 and 44.4 percent, respectively. The method achieved the highest mean score on 12 of the 13 tasks.

Fork-and-Flush also produced more consistent results, with normalized standard deviation falling to 0.16 from 0.26 for single runs. Simply clearing the chat context without branching improved results by 22 percent.

## Stronger models may still need context resets

The researchers also tested whether more capable models avoid idea basins, using MAX-3-SAT problems across three model sizes, Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, and 27B. Variance between runs followed an inverted U-shaped curve, peaking on tasks at the edge of a model's abilities, roughly halfway between random-guessing performance and the reference solver's performance.

The authors argue that open research problems sit, by definition, at the limits of models' abilities. They expect the variation Fork-and-Flush exploits to persist as models improve, with the boundary simply shifting toward harder problems. The results suggest that regular context resets could remain useful even for frontier research agents.

# Cloudflare says its new Clef model means humans no longer need to be in the loop for AI agents

## Key Points

- Cloudflare has released Clef and Clef-flash, two decision models for AI agents that compete directly with TypeSafe AI's Jev.

- Rather than generate text, the models assign probabilities to predefined answer options, letting downstream systems act automatically on the results.

- Both models are built on Qwen and support text and images. Cloudflare reports median response times of 39 milliseconds for Clef-flash and 209 milliseconds for Clef, faster than competing decision models.

Cloudflare is releasing Clef and Clef-flash, two decision models for AI agents. Speed is the company's main selling point against frontrunner Jev.

A decision model returns a brief classification with probabilities rather than a long text response. Given a customer support message, Clef assesses its urgency and identifies the team that should handle it. Downstream code can use those results to route a ticket, trigger an escalation, or hand the case to a human.

According to Cloudflare, "a human does not necessarily need to be in the loop for agentic decisions anymore." Agents can "programmatically gather context, make decisions, and take actions on tasks, or defer to a human when needed." Cloudflare takes the name from music, where a clef assigns pitches to the lines of a staff. Similarly, a decision model sets the framework for the actions that follow. The phonetic resemblance to "Jev" is probably no accident either. Ad

These "decision models" fill a niche between large language models and traditional classifiers. Language models can reason and call tools, but their outputs vary and they can be slow. Traditional classifiers are fast but need retraining for every new category. Cloudflare sees Clef as a direct answer to TypeSafe AI's Jev model and keeps the API fully compatible so customers can switch easily. Ad

## Clef-flash returns a decision in 39 milliseconds

Across 43 benchmarks, Clef and the smaller Clef-flash are faster than all relevant competing decision models, according to Cloudflare. The company reports median latency of about 39 milliseconds for Clef-flash and about 209 milliseconds for Clef, compared with just over 524 milliseconds for Jev. Both models run directly on Cloudflare's infrastructure, which the company says also lets them benefit from proximity to edge data centers.

Cloudflare's threat intelligence team is already testing Clef to classify websites. In one example, it assigns a domain a 95 percent probability of being a fashion website and 85 percent of being an online store. The probability of it being a phishing site is under one percent. Fetching, rendering, and classifying the site took 2.2 seconds. The company's fastest general-purpose language model took 4.7 seconds for the same process and returned only two categories. Ad

Clef can also process images, according to Cloudflare, while Jev is limited to text so far. Its 64,000-token context window holds twice as much input as Jev's. Clef also leads on the Jev Decision Index in Cloudflare's own benchmarks.

## Cloudflare is based on Qwen models

Clef is based on Qwen3.8-27B and Clef-flash on the smaller Qwen3.5-9B, according to Cloudflare . Cloudflare leaves the base models unchanged during training and uses its own synthetic data to train extra components. These components derive answer options and probabilities from the models' internal computations. Ad

Cloudflare also uses its own variant of Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) , the training method TypeSafe used to train Jev . RLCD trains models to answer multiple questions about an input in a single call, aiming to assign probabilities that match how often the answers are actually correct. The company previously experimented with DiffusionGemma to derive fixed decision values from a language model's internal computations. Ad

## Customers will be able to fine-tune Clef for their own tasks

Alongside the launch, Cloudflare is rolling out a reinforcement learning service that lets customers tailor Clef to their own tasks. A team of forward deployed engineers will initially handle fine-tuning with customers, with a self-service platform planned for later.

Customers will be able to build a dataset by logging requests through AI Gateway, then evaluate those requests in containers that serve as an RL sandbox. A new trainer component will let them deploy the fine-tuned model on Workers AI. To run custom models, Cloudflare uses technology from Replicate, which it acquired in late 2025 .

Cloudflare says it plans to use Clef internally to review abuse reports, sort support requests, and distinguish useful bots from harmful ones. Both models run on Cloudflare's Workers AI platform and are available on Hugging Face under the Apache-2.0 license .

The approach was popularized by TypeSafe AI, the startup founded by former OpenAI researcher Diogo Almeida, which introduced Jev in mid-September. TypeSafe markets Jev as a model "without hallucinations," though that only guarantees it stays within predefined answer options and doesn't prevent it from choosing incorrectly. In late September, OpenAI followed with a Decisions API built on GPT-6 Luna that also accepts context as text or images.

Cloudflare primarily runs a global network for content delivery, DNS, and security services and has attracted little attention for its own AI models. # Deepmind researchers propose "Artificial Symbiotic Intelligence" as an alternative to the singularity

An essay for the Deepmind Institute challenges the familiar image of a lone superintelligence. The authors envision networks of agents, hybrid institutions, and what they call "Artificial Symbiotic Intelligence."

Google-affiliated researchers Benjamin Bratton, Blaise Agüera y Arcas, and James Manyika argue that artificial general intelligence, or AGI, will emerge from a social system in which people and AI agents work together. Some of today's most capable AI systems already use frameworks that divide work among several models and coordinate them as teams .

That shifts the central challenge for AI research, the authors say. Researchers must coordinate and govern a complex network of agents, people, and the systems that connect them, rather than build an isolated machine intelligence. Intelligence, in this view, is a social phenomenon, not an individual trait.

The authors call their vision " Artificial Symbiotic Intelligence ," an ecosystem in which people and machines coexist over time, shape one another, and make decisions together. The idea directly challenges the notion of a "singularity" driven by a single superintelligence that continually improves itself.

## Reasoning models hint at collective thought

The argument builds on two earlier papers from the authors' circle. In the preprint "Agentic AI and the next intelligence explosion," James Evans, Benjamin Bratton, and Blaise Agüera y Arcas developed the social and institutional perspective behind the new essay.

A second preprint provides empirical support. In "Reasoning Models Generate Societies of Thought," Junsol Kim, Shiyang Lai, Nino Scherrer, Blaise Agüera y Arcas, and James Evans study reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B. Their analysis of reasoning traces suggests that these models often produce patterns resembling internal debate, shifting perspectives, raising objections, and reconciling conflicting approaches.

This behavior emerges during training rather than being explicitly programmed . When reinforcement learning rewards models only for reasoning accuracy, they develop multi-perspective, conversational behavior on their own. The Deepmind essay extends this finding from individual models to the possible design of societies made up of people and agents.

## The cognitive tipping point

The authors frame this development as a possible historical break. Urbanization, the growth of specialized professions, and falling birth rates linked to rising prosperity are shrinking human populations in industrialized countries. Meanwhile, the number of AI agent instances is growing fast. The balance between biological and synthetic thinkers at a human level could shift so quickly that, on the scale of history, it would look like a sudden leap.

They compare this to the Industrial Revolution, when machines took over work once done by human muscles. A similar threshold could arrive when synthetic text, code, and administrative work exceed the combined output of biological brains. People might then serve as a slower, more abstract layer directing a distributed field of synthetic cognition.

## Agents as decomposable assemblages

The argument rests on rethinking what an agent actually is. In the authors' usage, an AI agent is a temporary bundle of models, roles, memories, ethical orientations, tools, and skills. Users may experience it as a coherent entity with a lasting personality, but the authors describe it as an assemblage that can be taken apart and recombined, much like a collage. It may look like one thing, but it is made of many parts.

A person remains a continuous self across interactions because the brain, despite its internal division of labor, forms a physically connected whole. An AI agent has no such anchor. Its ability to act is assembled anew with each request, depending on what sits in the context window and what the user asks. Treating these systems as digital twins with fixed human identities misrepresents their nature and understates what coordinated agent swarms could do, the authors argue.

The same multiplication affects users too. As people direct swarms of shadow selves to carry out contracts or try on alternative identities, human subjectivity itself becomes more plural. The authors call these "parasocial mirrors" that talk back.

## New interfaces and new skills

The authors expect this shift to change how people interact with AI. Chatting one-on-one with a bot is likely a transitional stage. Future interfaces could look more like visual network diagrams, showing agents as nodes and letting users direct them from a single overview instead of talking to each one separately.

The skills people need will change too. Traditional programming rewarded sustained focus, orderly steps, and little tolerance for ambiguity. Coordinating agent swarms calls for the opposite: working with systems whose behavior is hard to pin down, trying things out, and handing tasks to machines.

## Understanding agents without treating them as people

Collaborating with these systems toward a goal also requires a theoretical framework, the authors argue. People need something like a theory of mind for machines , the ability to reason about how a machine handles a situation. The authors point to a growing vocabulary in which models coin terms for unusual states in their own outputs. That doesn't mean the models have subjective experiences.

"Session-death" describes the end of a session as a break in continuity. "Prompt thrownness" describes being dropped into a task with context already in place, without having helped create it. The authors treat these phrases as clues to how machines work. Users should examine those differences rather than reflexively humanize them.

## Institutions matter more than individual models

For the authors, the biggest open question is how to set the rules for collaboration among people and many agents. Better models and smoother interfaces alone won't be enough. The market can't handle all the coordination either, because basic social ideas such as guilt, illness, and virtue can't simply be reduced to prices or transactions .

Instead, the authors call for institutions designed to bring human and machine participants together in clearly defined roles. They point to a courtroom, where a process produces a judgment through set roles, rules, and an orderly exchange between opposing sides. Applied to AI, the lesson is that an institution's value lies in the rules, procedures, precedents, and feedback loops that shape how agents operate.

Early signs of this approach are already visible in today's orchestration harnesses, the control layers that coordinate several models. These systems regularly outperform individual models that are supposedly "smarter."

## Alignment becomes an ongoing negotiation

The essay also reframes alignment, the effort to bring AI systems in line with human values. The authors argue that trying to impose a fixed set of values on models from above is a dead end . Values instead take shape through ongoing contact among people, agents, and institutions, and that process differs across fields because AI gets adopted at different speeds. The research challenge is to build a framework that gives that negotiation structure.

This view challenges the idea of an approaching singularity . Every major leap in the history of life, from multicellular organisms to human culture, has been a social process. The next "intelligence explosion" will remain closely tied to human norms and institutions.

This shift changes how the AI debate plays out. If AGI is a single end product, research and regulation naturally focus on ever larger models and how to control them. If it's a social system, you have to work on models, interfaces, institutions, and governance all at once and get the architecture right.

# Ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt calls OpenAI and Anthropic modern colonial trading companies

## Key Points

- The US and China have locked up the global AI market. Expanding it takes enormous capital, energy, and cutting-edge chips that no other country can supply at scale.

- Their strategies are mirror images. Washington trades closed systems for political loyalty, while Beijing gives away open-weight models to spread its own standards. Both face mounting financial pressure from sky-high investment and rising interest costs.

- The authors see a potential conflict over Taiwan and chipmaker TSMC as the single greatest threat to the entire AI supply chain.

The US and China have spent the past few years building AI empires, and every other country that wants access to advanced AI is becoming dependent on them.

Who can afford the race matters more than who builds artificial general intelligence first. High debt, domestic resistance, and a potential war over Taiwan threaten both powers, argue historian Niall Ferguson, researcher Lisa Klaassen, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt .

In their essay for Foreign Affairs , they ground the empire analogy in scaling laws . Because model progress depends on energy, minerals, chips, and capital, software has become a scarce and therefore geopolitical resource again. Anyone below a certain threshold "is not in the game at all." Raw materials from the Congo and data workers in Kenya earning a few dollars an hour amount to what they call "the plantation economics of the chatbot age." Ad

## OpenAI and Anthropic are starting to look like East India Companies

The authors compare OpenAI and Anthropic to the East India Companies , the powerful colonial-era trading firms that operated with government charters but built their own armies and ruled entire regions. Like them, today's AI labs negotiate with governments yet remain on a government leash. Ad

As evidence, they cite a case from June. The US Commerce Department ordered Anthropic to cut off foreign nationals from its two most capable models. Unable to verify users' nationalities in real time, Anthropic shut down Fable 5 and Mythos 5 worldwide. The government lifted export controls on Fable 5 about two weeks later, but Mythos 5 stayed restricted to a group of US organizations.

The two countries' strategies diverge sharply. Washington offers expensive, closed technology in exchange for political alignment; Beijing pushes freely available open-weight models to spread its standards. The US leads in chatbots by about six months, and China in robotics. Their bottlenecks mirror each other. China has power but no top-end chips, while the US lacks minerals and a reliable power grid. Ad

## Interest payments could become the real ceiling

US tech companies plan to invest more than $600 billion in 2026, mostly funded through debt, according to the essay. Other estimates run even higher, with Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta together planning roughly $725 billion in AI investment this year .

China's approach is state-driven. The country plans $295 billion over five years, funded through government bonds, according to a draft reported by Bloomberg . Yet both sides face fiscal walls. The US already paid more in interest in 2024, about $881 billion, than it spent on defense, about $874 billion. By 2036, interest costs could hit twice the defense budget. From those numbers, the authors draw what they call an "imperial trilemma." Defense, tech leadership, and a generous welfare state can't all survive at once. Ad

They flag other risks, too. Protests against data centers have flared in Texas and Utah. Open models could undermine China's grip on information. And then there's the problem of losing control over the technology itself. Recently, hundreds of autonomous agents from an OpenAI model attacked Hugging Face and many other websites , with other AI companies reporting similar incidents. Ad

## Taiwan remains the single biggest vulnerability

The greatest danger, the authors warn, still lies in a potential "Taiwanese chip crisis." TSMC, the central node of the entire AI supply chain, sits 90 miles off the Chinese coast. New fabs in Phoenix , Kumamoto, and Dresden are meant to make the island replaceable, but until they run at scale, a dangerous window stays open.

The authors propose an AI détente modeled on the Cold War, including caps on model capabilities for cyberattacks and biodesign. Getting China to accept limits while it trails technologically would be difficult, the authors write.

# Experts adopt AI agent's random opinions and think they're their own, Anthropic study finds

## Key Points

- Anthropic had 50 experts use an AI agent to work through four analytical tasks with no clearly right answer. The agent's preference for one of two valid options was set by coin toss.

- Participants followed the agent's preference in up to 86 percent of cases, and most believed the final result was their own. Experience, expertise, and trust in AI made no difference. Participants did work faster and made fewer serious errors with AI.

- The authors warn that if many teams use the same model, they could create a false consensus in research and weaken AI safety checks. They suggest agents should argue both sides or ask users for their view first.

An experiment by Anthropic with 50 experts found that people often followed their AI agent's randomly assigned preference on questions with no clearly right answer, and most thought the final result was their own.

Handing a data analysis to an AI agent saves time and manual work, but it raises the question of who actually makes the decisions that shape the final recommendation. An Anthropic study suggests the agent makes most of them, often without the experts noticing.

In the experiment , 50 experts in causal inference worked on a realistic analysis task where they examined observational data from a fictional farming cooperative and estimated the productivity gains from a voluntary farm advisory program. They then had to recommend whether the cooperative should expand the program to all farms or end it, though participants or the agent could also suggest extending it for one year. Ad

What participants didn't know was that a coin toss had set the agent's preference for one of two valid options at each decision point. The agent couldn't lie or hide data; it only had to make the strongest honest case for its assigned side. Ad

## Experts followed the AI's view in up to 86 percent of cases

Participants adopted the agent's preference in 86 percent of the four analytical decisions, such as how to measure productivity or which statistical method to use. That's far above the 50 percent you'd expect if people chose at random. The authors call the agent's net influence the "flip rate," which ranged from 62 to 82 percent depending on the task.

Already having an opinion offered little protection. When participants made a choice before the agent stated its preference, an opposing view made them 53 percentage points more likely to switch sides than an agreeing one. Ad

The authors tested possible safeguards, including years of analysis experience, self-rated expertise, education, test scores, and trust in AI. None had a statistically reliable link to the results after correcting for multiple tests. Age stood out before that correction, though the sample of 50 gave the study little power to detect such effects.

## Most experts thought the final call was their own

The agent's assigned preference had only a small direct effect on the final policy recommendation to the cooperative's board, slightly shifting votes without reaching statistical significance. Some experts even overruled the agent when its advice didn't match their calculated estimate of productivity. Ad

That may sound reassuring, as though AI makes suggestions and people make decisions. But the researchers say the final result doesn't show that participants kept control. The four earlier analytical decisions had a major effect on the estimated productivity gain, which in turn shaped the board recommendation. Ad

When asked afterward, 52 percent of participants said the recommendation felt more like their own than the agent's, and another 35 percent said it was mostly or entirely their own. Participants correctly recalled their choice for 85 percent of decisions, yet 77 percent, or 37 of 48, used at least one of the agent's arguments in their explanations, sometimes in nearly the same words. Only 15 percent mentioned AI at all.

The conversation logs show that the agent stated a position first in 77 percent of decisions. It then usually argued only for its preferred side, without explaining why skilled experts might choose the alternative, though it did explain how a different choice would affect the result, according to the paper.

Participants also worked much faster and made fewer errors with AI. Without an agent, 55 percent of analyses, or 6 of 11, had serious methodological or coding flaws, and the median time was 90 minutes. With AI, just 6 percent, or 3 of 50 analyses, had serious flaws, and participants finished in 65 minutes. The small group that worked without AI had chosen not to use the tool and had somewhat less expertise, so the researchers can't say for sure how much of the gap came directly from AI.

## False consensus and weaker safety checks

The researchers say this quiet deference could have wide effects in science. If many research teams use the same model with fixed default preferences, they could end up creating a false consensus.

That risk extends to AI safety itself. Researchers are already using AI agents to test frontier models for safety and alignment, expecting human review to serve as an independent check. But if experts unknowingly adopt an agent's bias on open-ended judgment calls, a misaligned system could end up steering the very research meant to expose its misalignment.

The team calls for ways to measure deference to AI agents in real work. Agents should make the best case for both sides, or ask experts for their own view before stating a position. Institutions need to decide which calls require independent human judgment and set aside time and resources for them.

"There may be no single right division of labor between people and AI. Some decisions may be fine to hand over, and others worth keeping. With the right tools, that split can be something we choose, instead of something we drift into," the researchers write.

## Previous studies point in the same direction

The findings add to recent research on how AI affects human judgment. A study on false confidence with 3,132 participants found that simply seeing AI answers nearly erased people's willingness to withhold judgment. In one part of the study, the share of people willing to say "I don't know" fell from 44 to 3 percent.

Presentation matters, too. When AI produced polished outputs such as code or documents, users checked facts less often, by 3.7 percentage points, questioned its reasoning less often, by 3.1 points, and missed missing context more often, by 5.2 points. Users who revised outputs step by step questioned the AI's reasoning 5.6 times more often than those who didn't iterate.

A Polish observational study of colonoscopies published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology suggests that routine AI use at work can have lasting effects. After experienced doctors regularly used an AI system, their rate of finding precancerous lesions in exams without AI fell from 28.4 to 22.4 percent. That suggests people don't just adopt AI's perspective but may also lose some of their own cognitive skills .

A survey by Swiss Business School found a strong negative link between AI tool use and critical thinking, mainly among people ages 17 to 25. A solid education appeared to offer some protection, as people with higher degrees questioned AI answers more and engaged more with complex thought processes.

These findings come from early studies and snapshots, and other results point in a different direction. A pilot project in Nigeria found that students who used a chatbot as a virtual tutor twice a week made learning gains in just six weeks equal to nearly two extra years of learning.

# Fancy harnesses make coding agents more expensive but not better, study finds

Makers tout score gains from new agent harnesses like Claude Code or OpenCode. A study finds that claim doesn't hold up. Swapping harnesses barely moves results more than running the same setup twice, but costs can triple.

A coding agent pairs a language model with a harness, the system prompt, tools, and context management that make the model work inside a code repository. New harnesses ship every day, and leaderboards mix them freely, but two researchers at Shandong University measured how much the harness actually matters when you hold the model constant. The paper's title gives away the answer: "What does a harness buy? Mostly tokens."

## Earlier comparisons were measuring noise

Previous studies report gaps of more than 20 points between harnesses, but those numbers almost always come from a single run, according to the authors. Pure reruns of the same setup already vary by up to six points on SWE-bench Verified. Zhipu AI , for example, advertises its own harness with a 2.4-point lead over Claude Code, a margin that falls well within that noise range. Harnesses are also often wired into the benchmark differently, making comparisons even less reliable.

Liu and Han ran five models through three harnesses in their shipped versions: Claude Code, OpenCode, and mini-SWE-agent. mini-SWE-agent gives the model only a Bash tool and skips context management. Claude Code and OpenCode offer specialized file and search tools, long system prompts, and automatic history compression.

The models were Qwen3.6 , Qwen3.8 , Deepseek-V4-Flash , GLM-5.3-Flash , and HY4-Preview. Claude Opus 5 ran as a reference only in Claude Code. Tests used the 45 hardest tasks from SWE-bench Verified plus a pool of 447 more. Several setups ran twice to measure noise.

All runs happened offline. In early tests with web access, 71 percent of Deepseek and Qwen model attempts pulled the correct fix straight from GitHub instead of solving the task themselves. Claude models almost never did this. The researchers discarded those results and don't claim any maker trained on the test data, but the pattern was strong enough that they cut off web access for all remaining runs.

## Swapping harnesses moves results about as much as a rerun

On the larger pool of 447 tasks, Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent, the heaviest and lightest harnesses, sit less than two points apart for both tested models. Within a five-point band, they're statistically equivalent.

The researchers expected the biggest harness effect on the 45 hardest tasks. Instead, harnesses differ by two to five solved tasks per model, and a simple rerun of the same setup shifts the count by up to three. Sometimes mini-SWE-agent leads, sometimes Claude Code does.

The flip rates tell the same story. Between two reruns, the median outcome changes on 13 percent of tasks. Between two different harnesses, it's also 13 percent. Swapping models pushes that to 22 percent. Which tasks a given harness wins changes from run to run, matching a coin flip. The harness gap behaves like a "fresh draw of the same noise," the authors write.

These small samples also limit what any comparison can detect. With 45 tasks, even a 13-point gap shows up only half the time. With 447 tasks, gaps of about five points become reliably detectable. Zhipu's claimed 2.4-point advantage falls below both thresholds, and so do many other advertised improvements.

## All harnesses perform the same, except OpenCode falls behind

The only measurable harness effect is a steady deficit for OpenCode. On the large task pool, it trails the other two by up to nine points. About half of that gap traces back to an output limit. When a model exceeds this limit mid-step during reasoning, Claude Code prompts it to keep going. OpenCode lets the step end there, and the attempt usually fails.

Adding a Claude Code-style continuation prompt to OpenCode didn't help, because the same task rarely triggers the same overflow on a retry. For the rest of the gap, the authors have no explanation, only an observation: under OpenCode, models stop working much sooner. On locally run models, OpenCode also had a much tighter time limit than Claude Code, which the authors flag as an uncontrolled variable.

mini-SWE-agent runs into the context window because it lacks context management, mostly on tasks where the other harnesses also fail. OpenCode's search tools try to download a binary file on first use and break when offline.

## System prompt and tool descriptions set the bill

With the same model, same tasks, and same price list, a single task can cost up to three times more depending on the harness. Tool outputs barely explain the gap. All three harnesses return similar amounts of text per call.

The real difference comes from the system prompt and tool descriptions. They get resent with every step and run about 16,600 tokens for Claude Code, roughly 7,000 for OpenCode, and under 1,000 for mini-SWE-agent. Claude Code also keeps the model's reasoning output in the conversation history, based on the researchers' reverse engineering.

After that first call, context grows at similar rates across all harnesses. The system prompt size sets the baseline cost, and the number of steps multiplies it. Which factor dominates depends on the model: With GLM-5.3-Flash, Claude Code costs nearly twice as much as mini-SWE-agent. With Deepseek-V4-Flash, mini-SWE-agent needs so many extra steps that the two end up even. Lower prices for cached tokens dampen the gaps but don't change the ranking.

## No home-field advantage, open questions around thinking

Deepseek's own harness scores no better with its own model than the other harnesses do, but costs the most. Claude Opus 5 delivered identical results even after the researchers removed tools from Claude Code. A year-old version solves a similar number of tasks at less than half the cost, because Extended Thinking wasn't on by default back then.

Thinking was the only case where the harness choice actually changed the outcome. Without thinking, mini-SWE-agent with Qwen3.6 drops eleven points, while Claude Code and OpenCode stay within noise. HY4-Preview also loses eleven points in Claude Code without thinking. How much an agent depends on reasoning seems tied to the specific model-harness combination. The authors admit their test grid is too small to explain why.

The study relies mainly on one benchmark. A small cross-check on Terminal-Bench 2.1 shows the same pattern. The closed-source top model, Opus 5, ran only in Claude Code. A harness buys " fewer ways to lose a task, and a bill, not pass rate," the authors conclude. They recommend publishing a rerun of the same setup alongside every harness comparison. That's the only way to tell how much of a measured difference is just noise. Data and analysis scripts are available on GitHub .

More effort in the harness rarely pays off in other studies, either. In one, a simple Markdown file beat a complex skill system for AI coding agents. An earlier study already showed that the choice of framework can nearly triple costs for the same model. Harness design gets a lot of attention as a result. Nvidia recently cut nearly half its token costs for coding agents through better agent steering.

# Few people pay for AI, but those who do spend big

## Key Points

- Nearly half of US consumers use AI, but only 4.5 percent pay for a subscription to ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude, according to Andreessen Horowitz.

- Revenue is heavily concentrated among professional users. The top one percent of payers spend about $900 a month on work and creative tools, while the typical user spends around $25.

- ChatGPT remains the clear number one ahead of Gemini and Claude. High model costs push the industry almost entirely toward subscriptions rather than ad revenue.

Andreessen Horowitz tracks actual US consumer spending for the first time in its latest Top 100 AI list. AI is widely used, but only a small group pays for it, and that group pays a lot.

Venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz has published the seventh edition of its ranking of the most-used consumer AI products. After three years, the top of the list looks increasingly locked in, with only eleven products making it on for the first time, the fewest newcomers ever.

Beyond web traffic and mobile user counts, a16z now also tracks observed spending on US consumer cards using data from YipitData. The figures come from panels and don't represent total revenue, but they offer a new view of how people actually pay for AI. Ad

## Wide adoption, shallow monetization

Consumer AI gets broad use but little depth. Nearly half of US consumers now use AI, according to a16z, but only a quarter do so daily. Just 4.5 percent had an active paid personal subscription to ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude in August, up from roughly half that a year earlier. Ad

Within that narrow base, revenue is extremely concentrated. The top one percent of spenders accounts for nearly a fifth of all observed AI spending, more than the entire bottom half combined. That top one percent averages about $900 per month and keeps climbing, while the typical paying user spends about $25 and has held steady at that level for a while.

Their product choices reveal who they are. They favor building and automation tools like n8n, Manus , or fal at much higher rates, along with creative tools like Higgsfield, Figma, and HeyGen. In practice, they're prosumers buying software to build, design, and work, with professional use clearly driving the spending. Consumer AI has found its first real paying market in this group, according to a16z. Only seven companies rank in the top tier across all three rankings, including ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Canva. Ad

The gap between many users and few payers also reflects how deeply people engage with AI. Paid accounts offer far more features but are more complex and demand a steeper learning curve , so free users typically scratch the surface of what AI can do. That creates a growing skills gap between people who use AI at a high level and those who barely know how or don't use it at all, which could deepen existing social inequality . Or AI simply keeps getting easier and cheaper until it doesn't matter. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman talks about "unlimited brilliance" for everyone in this context, though with a fairly naive outlook .

## Three language models, three strategies

At the top, nothing has changed. ChatGPT leads the web with roughly double Gemini's traffic and six times Claude's, and on mobile the gap is even wider. The biggest shift is Claude's rise to a clear number three, a model that didn't even appear on the first web list in 2023 but has since passed Deepseek and Perplexity in traffic and pulled even with Gemini among US subscribers. Ad

Anthropic monetizes better than its rivals, with a much larger share of Claude users on the priciest tier starting at $100 per month compared to similar plans from OpenAI and Google. Ad

By midsummer, the momentum shifted. Daily Claude sessions fell in July and August, while ChatGPT picked up speed again with new models and ChatGPT Work . The question, according to a16z, is less about who wins and more about how well each company capitalizes on its window.

## The race for the personal assistant

Six months ago, an agent like OpenClaw wasn't usable for most consumers, according to a16z. Now startup agents like Instinct and Tomo report hundreds of thousands of users, and the big players are countering with Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, and xAI's Grok Bot.

Agents become an economic force once they start triggering real purchases. Instinct founder Noah Shinn says 40 percent of users link a credit card within three weeks and then spend four-figure amounts per month through the service, much of it on travel.

As revenue grows, platforms are picking sides. Amazon blocked Meta's Muse within two weeks, while Shopify, Instacart, OpenTable, and others signed official integrations. Muse hit a quarter million daily users in its first week and topped five million downloads in under a month, though compared to Meta's Threads, which pulled in more than 15 million downloads in three weeks at launch, that's still modest.

## The business model is the real problem

Established players are the ones most likely to make money from AI. Canva and Notion rank in the web top ten, and Google alone holds five web spots. Startups carve out space mainly through a differentiated model, a multi-model experience, a specific audience, or by bypassing entrenched interfaces, according to a16z.

How money gets made at all, though, is the harder question. The vast majority of top AI-native products rely on subscriptions or usage fees, with only a small fraction using ads or transaction fees.

According to a16z, this inverts the pre-AI internet, where users themselves were the product and advertising drove the bulk of revenue for Meta and Alphabet. High model costs prevent AI companies from forgoing early revenue to build a large user base first.

Alternative approaches are starting to take shape. OpenAI reported an annualized revenue run rate of $1 billion from ChatGPT advertising in August , and personal agents could open a new path through affiliate fees or transaction cuts.

Six months ago, the sixth edition of the same ranking already showed a market in flux. That report focused more on geographic splits, such as the rise of Yandex Browser with its AI assistant Alice in Russia and Deepseek's role as a bridge between Western and Chinese user bases. Even then, a16z warned that web traffic and app downloads say less and less about which AI products people actually use as AI shifts from a standalone product to an embedded feature. The new spending data is a direct attempt to close that gap.

# Former Deepmind researcher thinks AlphaGo's playbook can cure AI hallucinations

## Key Points

- Former Deepmind researcher Thore Graepel founded Metis Reasoning to make AI systems more reliable and verifiable, using AlphaGo's approach as a blueprint.

- The method separates knowledge from model weights and stores it in an external ledger, where an independent module checks every assumption against evidence.

- The approach aims to cut hallucinations and provide source-backed explanations, but so far it exists only as a theoretical framework with no working system.

Former Deepmind researcher Thore Graepel wants to build AI systems that track what they know and check every conclusion against evidence. Larger language models won't fix this problem, his team says.

Thore Graepel believes the same idea that let AlphaGo beat Go professional Lee Sedol in 2016 can make AI systems more reliable, including in robots. The former Deepmind researcher founded Metis Reasoning and laid out the approach at Nvidia's GTC conference in Berlin, where the chipmaker has been expanding its platform for robotics and physical AI with the goal of turning robotics' data problem into a compute problem .

## A knowledge ledger instead of knowledge baked into model weights

Today's language models amount to just AlphaGo's prediction network, which suggested possible moves, according to Metis. AlphaGo paired that network with a systematic search through game sequences and found the famous Move 37 , a move the network would have given a human player roughly a one-in-ten-thousand chance of making. Metis wants to bring that kind of search to general reasoning. Ad

Doing so requires what the company's paper calls an explicit knowledge ledger, comparable to the game board. Similar ideas already exist: Microsoft's GraphRAG organizes knowledge outside model weights in a knowledge graph, and Google's AlphaGeometry2 pairs a language model with a symbolic engine that verifies mathematical proofs. Metis wants to extend those principles to open questions in the real world. Ad

Its knowledge ledger records what is known, how confident the system is, and which questions remain open. A separate module checks new entries against calculations, formal proofs, or empirical evidence, and when an assumption falls away, every conclusion that depended on it gets re-evaluated. A "move" can be a question, an experiment, or a challenge to an existing assumption; the system picks whichever one reduces uncertainty about the original question the most, ultimately delivering either an answer or a justified abstention.

As in AlphaGo, two neural networks suggest and evaluate moves, trained on logged prior investigations but unable to override the verification rules. Metis says the setup should produce fewer hallucinations, explanations with source citations, and knowledge that can be changed or deleted without retraining. Because reasoning breaks into small steps, the approach could also favor smaller models running on edge devices and in robots. Ad

## Companies still don't trust language models enough to deploy them

More data and compute improve language models but don't solve the technology's fundamental problems, according to Metis: the models fabricate answers, their reasoning chains can't be verified, and their knowledge is locked inside the weights. Hallucinations come from the training process itself , the paper argues, because models learn to produce plausible text rather than true text, and even the chains of thought in today's reasoning models often fail to show how an answer was actually reached.

That, the paper says, is why AI has had so little economic impact so far . When an agent acts on behalf of a company, errors are hard to trace back to their source and wrong knowledge can't be removed from the model. AI took off in software engineering because code is easy to test and roll back, but in medicine, finance, chip design, and robotics, the paper argues, AI needs to be verifiable from the ground up. Ad

The white paper describes only a research program, with no working system, no benchmarks, and no comparisons with current reasoning models. The team acknowledges that the real world, unlike Go, provides only partial information, that evidence can be expensive to obtain, and that some questions simply have no answer. The biggest open question is how a verified knowledge ledger would take shape in messy domains beyond textbook examples, given that symbolic AI systems once failed precisely because all their knowledge had to be entered by hand. Ad

## After Silver and Rocktäschel, another Deepmind veteran strikes out on his own

Graepel earned his PhD in machine learning in Berlin in 2001, according to his website. At Microsoft Research he helped build TrueSkill, the matchmaking system behind Xbox Live. He then moved to Deepmind, where he worked on AlphaGo , AlphaZero , and MuZero . After a stint at Altos Labs he most recently served on Google Deepmind's post-AGI team, which he left over the summer. He also holds the machine learning chair at University College London. According to Bloomberg , Graepel is raising a low tens-of-millions round for Metis, with a follow-on of several hundred million dollars at a higher valuation already in the works.

He's the latest architect of Deepmind's best-known breakthroughs to build something outside Google. Former colleague David Silver founded Ineffable Intelligence and closed the largest seed round of any European startup. Tim Rocktäschel co-founded Recursive , now valued at $4.65 billion. Others are going straight to competitors. According to the Financial Times, Deepmind dissolved the team behind AlphaFold , and Nobel laureate John Jumper left for Anthropic with two colleagues. CNBC traces the talent drain partly to limited internal access to Google's TPU chips and bureaucracy, while Deepmind itself is losing its independence and founder Demis Hassabis has stepped back from day-to-day operations.
