# Gemini 4 Argon is now available worldwide as Google's most capable frontier model

Google is rolling out Gemini 4 Argon globally, making its new flagship AI model available to developers, businesses, and consumers starting today.

Gemini 4 Argon is accessible through the API in AI Studio and the Gemini platform , according to Google. Google AI Ultra subscribers can use the model in Google Antigravity , while AI Ultra and Pro subscribers get access through the Gemini app and Google Search's AI mode .

Not everyone benefits equally, though. Free Gemini users and paying Plus subscribers now only have access to the weaker Flash models under a new model tier structure . Argon replaces the Gemini Pro class as Google's new frontier series. Google says more Gemini 4 models will follow, which likely means updated Flash variants that would eventually trickle down to free and Plus users as well. Internally, Google is reportedly already testing a potential successor codenamed " Carbon ," which is supposed to outperform Argon at coding in particular. Ad

Pricing and benchmark results remain as previously reported : $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens at the introductory rate, with a 95 percent discount on cached inputs. Argon holds the top spot on the Vals Index, but it still trails Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 in independent overall rankings. And because Google waited roughly two weeks to ship, it now also sits behind Meta's Muse Wonder Full , which launched just yesterday. Ad

*Google doesn't state this figure explicitly but says the cache is 95 percent cheaper than the regular input token price.

## Google says Argon turned months of internal engineering into weeks

Google shared some internal numbers with the launch, though they're self-reported. Software engineers using Argon increased agent-driven code submissions by more than 35 percent, while code rollbacks dropped by nearly a third, the company says. Ad

In the Chromium project, Argon helped the Chrome team complete an architectural refactor across hundreds of files within the 40-million-line codebase. Work that would have taken months was finished in a few weeks. For users, the payoff is that web pages can move between tabs, sidebars, and floating windows without needing to reload.

Working with Google's open-source Agent Development Kit , Argon ran autonomously overnight and found optimizations that cut session preparation time by 40 percent and sped up cold imports by 21 percent. Inference speed for the open Gemma models on an A100 via vLLM jumped by a factor of 2.85, from roughly 37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second. The changes are visible in upstream pull requests . Ad

Argon can also generate complex 3D models, games, and animations in pure code that run directly in the browser. One demo features a raytracing engine written entirely in Python with no external libraries. Google published the source code . Ad

In the demo below, Argon starts from a single image in Antigravity and controls Blender via MCP in an autonomous loop. It modeled gothic architecture and set up audio-reactive lighting to produce a finished 3D scene, Google says.

3D remains a weak spot for Meta's Muse models, which according to Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang were not specifically trained for 3D demo games.

## Google offers 10,000 researchers free access and claims its strongest safety record yet

Google is also offering 10,000 researchers the highest usage tier of Google Antigravity free for six months. Spots are awarded on a rolling basis depending on eligibility, capacity, and selection. Applications are open now.

Cybersecurity defenders can apply separately for the Fairwind program , which grants access to Argon without cyber safeguards. Google plans to expand the program to hundreds of additional partners.

On the safety side, Google calls Argon's architecture its strongest to date. External red teaming in the bio domain bypassed fewer than 1 percent of tested safety checks, and on an adversarial set, violations dropped by nearly half compared to earlier Gemini models.

On agent alignment, attempts to take unauthorized shortcuts fell to 2 percent. An automated misalignment monitor analyzes the agent's reasoning and actions in real time.

Argon also scored the lowest attack rate on the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, with a successful attack rate of just 0.7 percent across 15 adaptive attempts. In the previous Gray Swan test , GPT-6 Astra hit 8.5 percent and Claude Opus 5 came in at 4.8 percent. Google's write-up doesn't make clear whether the exact same tests were used, though. More safety details are available in the model card .

# Google Deepmind releases Gemini 4 Carbon just two weeks after Argon with gains across the board

## Key Points

- Just two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Carbon, its next frontier model. Carbon tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 with 59 points, up from Argon's 50.

- Google says Carbon is built for multi-day, autonomous development workflows. It's closing the gap fast in Artificial Analysis's Coding Agent Index (59 points vs. Argon's 50) but still trails Claude Opus 5.5 (62 points).

- Because of its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, Carbon is going through the U.S. government's voluntary pre-testing process and will only be available to selected security experts at first. Pricing stays the same as Argon.

Google Deepmind shipped Gemini 4 Carbon just two weeks after Argon, and the new model takes the top spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.

Carbon scores 59 points on the recently updated version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , while predecessor Argon trails at 50. Beyond general gains in agentic tasks and programming, Google highlights capabilities spanning the full cyber defense lifecycle, from detecting and validating vulnerabilities to patching them.

## Built for multi-day coding sessions

Google Deepmind says it designed Carbon for "much harder, long-horizon engineering problems" that demand persistent agentic workflows. Internal teams ran the model for multiple days straight, during which it worked through dead ends on its own and handled complex, multi-step tasks like root-cause analysis and subtle bug fixes in large codebases and low-level software, Google claims. Ad

Google also reports improvements in scientific reasoning, multimodal understanding, and full-stack web development based on user feedback. Higher-quality outputs and artifacts in web development pushed Carbon up 89 Elo points on the WebDev Arena , where it sits in fourth place at 1,769. Ad

On Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection benchmark, Carbon pushed the attack success rate from 0.7 percent with Argon down to 0.0 percent, blocking every tested manipulation attempt according to Google. That doesn't mean prompt injection is solved, but the test appears to be saturated.

## Independent evaluations back up Google's numbers

According to Artificial Analysis , Carbon at its highest reasoning tier ("high") leads the Intelligence Index v5 mainly because of top scores in complex reasoning, knowledge retrieval, and scientific tasks, taking first place in four of the index's nine individual evaluations. Ad

In agentic coding on Antigravity, Carbon still trails Claude Code with Opus 5.5 by three points, despite jumping from 53 to 59 compared to Argon. In agentic knowledge work on AA-Briefcase, Carbon (high) gains 126 points over Argon (high, 1,483 Elo) to reach 1,609 Elo, driven by presentation quality (+293 Elo to 1,598) and analytical quality (+120 Elo to 1,671). It still falls behind Kimi K3.1 Pro (1,678 Elo), Muse Wonder (max, 1,659 Elo), and Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 1,638 Elo).

Answer accuracy rises from 48 to 58 percent compared to Argon, while the hallucination rate climbs from four to 11 percent. That's higher but still the second-lowest in the ranking. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max) each sit at 50 percent. Ad

The evaluation platform Vals AI puts Carbon in second place at 70.36 percent accuracy, behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (70.85 percent) and ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (70.18 percent) and Argon in fourth (69.24 percent), all at lower cost. Ad

On Vals.ai, Carbon also leads both the Finance Index and the Legal Research benchmark. In legal research, Vals AI recorded roughly 45 percent more cited sources, more frequent tool calls, and longer responses than Argon.

But tasks in the Finance and Tax Agent benchmark take more than twice as long as with Argon, and in Legal Research, Carbon averages more than 50 minutes per task. The model generates 2.3 times as many reasoning tokens and 64 percent more output tokens than Argon, though that's still less than half the output token count of Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5.

On Arena.ai , Gemini 4 Carbon (High) takes the Text Arena lead with 1,528 points, edging past Argon (1,520). In the Agent Arena, the model places second across more than 21,900 real sessions, ahead of GPT-6 Astra and Fable-5.1, with a net improvement of 16.2 percent and the highest steerability score (+18.6 percent). Its median task cost of $1.80 is 72 percent below first-place Claude Opus 5.5 (Max).

In the WebDev category of the Code Arena, Carbon reaches 1,768 points (89 ahead of eleventh-place Argon) for fourth overall, just two behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (xHigh, 1,770). That places it on the Pareto curve across all three disciplines.

## Carbon leads security benchmarks without guardrails

For several security tests, Google ran the model without safety guardrails. On SEC-bench Pro , which measures autonomous vulnerability discovery in real-world software, Carbon scores 88.2 percent and leads all tested models. On ExploitGym , which tests whether a system can turn discovered vulnerabilities into working exploits, the model reaches 54.8 percent. Carbon also holds a wide first-place lead in writing fixes on CWE-Bench .

Google also cites internal results that can't be independently verified. On in-house benchmarks, Carbon reportedly produces secure code more than twice as often as Argon, and in tests by Google's Chrome team, it performed more than ten times better at writing security patches than the frontier model of an unnamed competitor.

## Security experts get access first

Google is rolling out the model gradually and participating in the U.S. government's pre-release testing process, citing Carbon's advanced security capabilities. Selected cybersecurity experts get access first starting this week. Through Google Deepmind's Fairwind Program , access will expand to more trusted partners after that.

The company plans to open the model to developers, businesses, and consumers through its product interfaces after collecting more feedback and adjusting the safety guardrails.

## Key Points

- Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Argon, its latest flagship model that closes the gap with frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic, beating some of them on key benchmarks.

Google unveiled Gemini 4 Argon, its new frontier model that closes the gap with rivals from OpenAI and Anthropic, beating some of them on key benchmarks. While it may not clearly lead the pack, it is relatively cheap for a frontier model, at least at the introductory price.

Argon is Google's first frontier model in more than seven months, following Gemini 3.1 Pro. It puts the ad giant back among the top three AI labs, though Anthropic likely still holds the lead. After a difficult and drawn-out development period that saw the already-announced Gemini 3.5 frontier model skipped entirely, Google is back in the race.

## Most users will have to wait

Argon is initially going to a group of "trusted cyber defenders" as part of the Fairwind program . They and Google's internal teams will get the model without cyber guardrails. Google justifies the gradual rollout with a "phased approach" that AI capabilities at this level require. The company is also taking part in the US government's voluntary program that gives agencies access to new models before public release. Ad

Feedback from early testers will feed into the model's safety mechanisms. Only after that does Google plan to open Argon up to developers, businesses, and consumers, starting with paying API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers. The company hasn't given a date, saying only "as soon as possible." Ad

Pricing is already set, at least as an introductory rate: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Cached input tokens cost 95 percent less, working out to about 10 cents per million. Gemini 3.8 Flash had a 90 percent cache discount. That puts Google well below other frontier models on raw token price, though not on token consumption (see below).

*Google doesn't state this figure explicitly but says the cache is 95 percent cheaper than the regular input token price. Ad

Google also raised the output limit from 64,000 to one million tokens, calling it an industry first. The idea is that if the model can generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single trajectory, it can think through hard problems more thoroughly and solve them in one pass. To support this, Google is adding a new "Long Decode Continuation" feature to the Gemini API. It pauses long responses and resumes them through follow-up requests so reasoning doesn't hit a timeout.

The input context window stays at one million tokens. Argon accepts text, images, video, and audio as input but only outputs text. Ad

## Independent tests show Argon matching GPT-6 Astra but burning more tokens

Artificial Analysis provides an early independent assessment. At its highest available reasoning level, "High," Gemini 4 Argon scores 53 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. That ties it with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra (max) and Claude Fable 5.1, and puts it one point ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol (max). Ad

Anthropic's models still lead. Claude Opus 5.5 sits at 58 points and Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 56. Compared to Google's last frontier model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Argon jumped 23 points. "High" is typically the top reasoning tier for Gemini models, though a special "Deep Think" mode is sometimes supported as well.

At the current promo price, one Intelligence Index task costs $1.99. That's 60 percent of GPT-6 Astra's cost ($3.26) but 2.7 times more expensive than GPT-6.1 Sol. Once the discount ends, the cost rises to $3.98, about 20 percent above GPT-6 Astra. The price advantage comes from lower token rates, not from efficiency. Argon uses an average of 62,000 output tokens per task, while GPT-6 Astra needs only 27,000.

Argon also made significant gains on agentic tasks, which according to Artificial Analysis have been a weak spot for Gemini models. On AutomationBench-AA, the Artificial Analysis variant, it takes first place at 77.5 percent, six points ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max). On Terminal Bench 4, it hits 57 percent, a 53-point jump over Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. That still leaves it behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (64 percent), Claude Opus 5.5 (60 percent), and GPT-6 Astra (59 percent).

Artificial Analysis also highlights Argon's low hallucination rate. On AA-Omniscience, a benchmark that tests factual knowledge and honest handling of knowledge gaps, Argon's hallucination rate is 15 percent. GPT-6 Astra (max) comes in at 51 percent and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 54 percent. Argon is far more likely to admit it doesn't know an answer rather than guess wrong. Its accuracy, however, reaches only 50 percent, five points below Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and 13 points below GPT-6 Astra (max, 63 percent). On the benchmark's overall score, Argon lands at 42 points, roughly even with GPT-6 Astra (43) and GPT-6.1 Sol (42).

Google's own benchmark results paint a rosier picture. Argon leads in most of those benchmarks, sometimes by wide margins.

Argon also leads the Vals Index . At 68.9 percent, it takes first place according to Vals AI, making it the first Gemini model to top the index. Argon finishes in the top five on 20 of 22 tested benchmarks, with particular strength in finance, law, coding, and security. In this test, though, the mid-tier model Sonnet 5.5 also outranks Anthropic's top model Opus 5.5, so take it with a grain of salt.

As always, AI models have to prove themselves in real-world use, and performance depends not just on the model itself but also on the software wrapped around it. That's Google's weak spot right now: compared to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT Work, the Gemini app still lags behind.

## Argon tops the human preference rankings for text

On Arena.ai , where humans rate model outputs in head-to-head comparisons, Argon performs well. In the Text Arena, Gemini 4 Argon (High) takes first place with 1,525 points, 20 points ahead of Claude Opus 4.6 (High) in second. That makes it a strong contender for writing tasks, especially after a long drought of competitive writing models and Opus 5.5 still not matching Opus 4.6 in human preference rankings. Google's previous model, Gemini 3.8 Flash (High), had been in eleventh place.

According to Arena, Argon leads in coding, hard prompts, instruction following, longer queries, and creative writing. It also ranks first across all evaluated professional fields, as well as for queries in English, Chinese, Russian, and non-English queries overall.

Web development results are more modest. In Code Arena: WebDev, Argon scores 1,679 points and lands in eighth place. That's a 96-point improvement over Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) and a jump from 29th, but it doesn't crack the top spots.

On price-to-performance, Arena puts Argon ahead of the field. At a blended rate of $8 per million tokens, Argon shifts the Pareto frontier of the Text Arena and is currently the most cost-efficient model in the ranking.

# Google researchers find a way to keep self-improving AI agents from memorizing their tests

AI agents that keep optimizing their own working environment quickly tend to overspecialize on their test tasks. A new method from Google Cloud AI Research and several universities aims to prevent that while also cutting compute costs.

Modern AI agents wrap a fixed language model in a so-called harness , a framework of prompts, workflows, tools, memory, and logic that controls what the model sees at each step.

The harness decides whether an agent reads the right file before changing it, whether it recovers from a mistake, and whether it delivers its results cleanly. According to a new research paper, much of the recent progress in agents comes from work on the harness, not from new models.

Until recently, this was done by hand. People reviewed failed runs and patched the harness manually. Newer methods automate the loop by having a language model rewrite the harness itself, again and again, based on feedback from the test tasks.

The researchers call this a practical form of recursive self-improvement. The system produces feedback that it uses to optimize the harness, which in turn controls the system's own behavior.

## Self-optimization leads agents to memorize their test tasks

The paper shows that this self-optimization comes with a catch. Because the agent keeps working on the same limited set of test tasks, it ends up memorizing them. Its scores on the training tasks go up, while gains on new, unseen tasks shrink or disappear entirely.

The researchers say this happens in several ways. The search memorizes patterns that only fit one particular benchmark, favors candidates that score well purely by chance, and piles on unnecessary complexity that raises the test score without making the agent any better.

Other methods mostly improve on the training tasks, but little of that carries over to unseen benchmarks. RRSI raises scores there in all three domains. | Image: Google

## Shrinking edit budgets and a strict critic keep the harness general

RRSI (Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses) works on both ends of the optimization loop while leaving the harness fully editable. When the system proposes new changes, a budget caps how many independent edits a candidate can bundle at once.

That budget shrinks over time. Early rounds allow larger rewrites, while later rounds only permit small changes that can be clearly traced to a result. The system also keeps track of earlier attempts so it doesn't keep chasing the same failed ideas. When progress stalls, it deliberately experiments with parts of the harness it hasn't touched yet.

RRSI reins in self-optimization at two points, when proposing new changes and when deciding which of them become a permanent part of the harness. | Image: Google

When it comes to picking changes, a critic reviews every proposal and throws out any that hardcode task names, solutions, or other benchmark-specific tricks. Another rule only accepts higher compute costs if they come with a measurable performance gain. Components that no longer help get removed.

## Giving up training gains pays off on new tasks

The researchers tested RRSI on eight benchmarks spanning coding, agentic office work, and engineering design. The underlying model, Claude Opus 4.8 , stayed frozen throughout. The team compared RRSI with the unmodified baseline harness and four recent optimization methods.

According to the paper, RRSI gains up to 14.1 points on the tasks it was trained on and up to 4.7 points on five benchmarks it never saw. It also uses about 30 percent fewer tokens at runtime than the unregularized version. Overall performance never fell below the baseline on any of the unseen benchmarks, which typically happens with a harness that has memorized its tasks.

The RRSI harness also improves on every task outside the training set, with the biggest gain of 4.7 points on JobBench. | Image: Google

Every method did well on the training tasks, but the results flipped on new ones. Two methods even ended up below the baseline harness. RRSI posted the smallest training gain of all the variants and was the only method that landed well above the baseline on unseen tasks. The guardrails are meant to produce exactly this tradeoff.

Among the optimized harnesses, RRSI needs the fewest tokens and steps and performs best on new tasks, though the unmodified baseline harness is even leaner. | Image: Google

## Harnesses optimized on one model also help weaker ones

A coding harness optimized with Gemini 3.5 Flash raised the accuracy of the much weaker Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite from 11.2 to 14.6 points without any modifications. The mechanisms the system found don't depend on the capability of the model used to discover them.

The authors note that their study only covers harnesses built around frozen models and doesn't address cases where the model weights change.

They conclude that self-improvement only makes AI agents reliably more capable when repeated feedback gets turned into lasting changes. The code is available on GitHub .

Manually designed harnesses often don't generalize to new tasks, as tests on ARC-AGI-3 have shown. With a purpose-built harness, Opus 4.6 scored 97.1 percent in a familiar environment and 0 percent in an unfamiliar one. Nvidia recently presented SoL-Pi , a related method in which a research agent automatically rebuilds the harness of coding agents. It cuts token use by up to 49 percent without a noticeable drop in performance.

Shortly before that, Google had agents "dream" about past search runs to improve their search strategy. That work also leaves the model itself unchanged.

# Google says self-improving AI isn't anywhere close

Google engineer Haydn Belfield says self-improving AI remains far off, even as significant automation is already taking hold.

Google Deepmind has seen no measurable acceleration of AI research driven by AI itself, according to Belfield. That doesn't mean significant automation isn't happening already: AI now writes more than 75 percent of production code. But about 88 percent of code changes still need human oversight or review, and every change is reviewed by a human before submission, according to Belfield. The share of code changes fully delegated to AI rose from 7.5 to 11.9 percent.

The more complex and time-consuming a task gets, the less likely AI is to handle it on its own . Across 1,389 internal Argon agent runs, the success rate without human input dropped sharply as complexity increased. Humans remain essential for creative research, novel experiment design, diagnosing subtle training instabilities, and long-term planning, Belfield said . A survey of twelve senior Deepmind researchers confirmed the pattern, with automation running highest for well-defined, verifiable tasks and lowest for open-ended scientific ideation. Ad

On Deepmind's in-house benchmark RE-Bench, which includes 74 realistic ML engineering tasks, Argon solves about half of them. That's a big jump from Gemini 3.7 Flash at 27 percent, but it's still far from the near-perfect performance full automation would require. Ad

To track progress systematically, the team built a General Capability Index (GCI) covering 123 models and 92 benchmarks. Gemini model capabilities are growing at a steady pace of about 0.1 GCI points per month, with no significant change in speed. The team attributes Gemini 4 Argon sitting slightly above the trend line to more compute and organizational investment rather than AI-driven acceleration.

The team currently rates the risk from AI-driven research automation as low but is building the measurement infrastructure to track signs of acceleration going forward. Ad

## Key Points

- From simple inputs like photos or sketches, the system builds simulations where robots can practice movements before real-world deployment.

It came up with 77 tasks, from righting toppled objects to clearing the table, and generated more than 4,500 training episodes for a control model. Argon can work from other sources, too. From a recording of a teleoperated robot, it builds a simulation designed to look the same and replicate the same force readings at the fingertips. From a first-person video of a human performing a grasping task, the model maps hand and finger movements onto a virtual humanoid with five-fingered hands.

Even a ballpoint pen sketch works. One drawing shows a humanoid robot knocking down a pyramid of boxes with a ball, and Argon turns it into a simulation that calculates a throwing motion to topple all six boxes without the robot falling over. Ad

## Argon directs an AI video model to plan robot actions

One demo plays out entirely inside an AI-generated video. Gemini Omni is a video world model that generates clips showing how a scene changes when something happens in it, and Argon acts as the director. It writes timestamped instructions describing what the hands should do, like sliding a Scrabble tile to the center of the table. Gemini Omni generates a video from those instructions, and Argon then checks individual frames and adjusts the next command. The goal is to arrange five scattered letter tiles to spell "ARGON," and after 33 steps, they're in the right order.

In a separate demo with a simple robot arm, Argon had to place a Lego brick into a wooden box and improve its own performance over time. When attempts failed, the prompt told Argon to review its own logs and camera images, find the cause, and retry after applying a verified fix. The first run took just under a minute, and the second was much faster at 23 seconds, though the brick clipped the edge of the box. On the third try, it landed dead center after about 17 seconds. Ad

Google also wants Argon to serve research. Given a single prompt per paper, it recreates published robotics experiments as interactive simulations that run in the browser. Google says 68 such sandboxes have been built so far, including robot soccer and a humanoid robot on a skateboard. Ad

The ERQA benchmark (Embodied Reasoning Question Answering) tests how well AI models understand and solve physical and spatial problems in 3D environments. The test used 400 questions with no helper tools, so models had to solve everything through reasoning alone. Argon scores 87 percent according to Google, ahead of all other frontier models. The runner-up, Claude Opus 5.5, hit 82.3 percent, about five percentage points behind. GPT-6 Astra followed at 81 percent, and Claude Fable 5.1 trailed at 74 percent, 13 points back.

The AA-Robotics benchmark from Artificial Analysis, published a day later, tells a different story. In that test, language models directly control a real robot arm across eight tasks, and Argon landed third with 55 out of 100 points, behind GPT-6 Astra at 69 and GPT-6.1 Sol at 65.

## Argon also reviews training data quality

Beyond controlling robots and building simulations, Argon is meant to evaluate training data. In a video just over two minutes long showing a dual-arm robot folding an origami fox, the model breaks the sequence into sub-steps and flags pauses and botched grips. Those segments are then weighted less during training. In another video of a human sorting rings, Argon traced where the task progresses, stalls, or goes backward.

Google also showed a more playful use case built around a classic weighing puzzle . Among twelve identical-looking balls, one is heavier or lighter than the rest. Argon built a simulation with two robot arms and a balance scale, reading the scale's tilt from camera images alone. It finds the odd ball in three weighings or fewer.

## The real scaffolding lives in the prompts

Google published detailed example prompts for the demos, and they put some of the bigger claims into perspective. For righting an overturned cup, described as "zero-shot," Argon receives a camera image with a centimeter grid overlay and pre-built commands like "grasp" or "lower until contact." For the simulations, there are long prohibition lists to keep the model from taking shortcuts, like simply copying measured sensor values. Google doesn't share failure rates for individual demos in the blog post, and the 75 percent success rate lacks any mention of how many total attempts it's based on.

Argon is available now in Google AI Studio and the development environment Antigravity , but only for Google AI Ultra subscribers. Developers can also access the model through the paid tier of the Gemini API .

Google had released Gemini 4 Argon globally just days earlier. For robotics, the company had already introduced Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6 , a model for spatial perception and task planning. In the "Standard Harness," which only allows simple notes between rounds, Argon drops to 49.8 percent at low reasoning for $5,800. This gap traces back to a July 2026 dispute when OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol beat Claude Opus 5 on ARC-AGI-3 using two API settings . Ad

Performance varies by domain, though. According to Epoch AI , Argon leads several knowledge, agent, and vision benchmarks, but early estimates put it in eighth on the Math ECI and sixth on the Software Engineering Index (SWE ECI). Ad

# GPT-6-Astra solves 49 of 50 physics research problems at $2.40 apiece

A new benchmark shows the best AI agents can solve theoretical physics calculations as accurately as leading specialists in each subfield. The researchers behind it say a missing sense of "taste" is one reason breakthroughs haven't followed yet.

Thirty-five researchers from institutions including the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS), Harvard University, KU Leuven, and Google DeepMind have released TheoPhysEval . The benchmark contains 50 unpublished research problems in theoretical physics with verifiable answers. According to the authors, a leading expert in the relevant subfield would need about a day or less to solve a typical problem without AI help. Specialists from neighboring fields would take much longer.

The team tested commercially available AI agents and gave them no human hints. GPT-6-Astra, running in OpenAI's Codex coding environment, came out on top. It found the right answer for 49 of 50 problems, or 98 percent, at an average cost of under $3 per problem and just under $116 for the whole benchmark.

## The benchmark tests routine research work, not grand challenges

The collection deliberately leaves out major open questions and focuses on what the authors call "turn-the-crank" problems, where researchers apply known methods to a slightly modified question. Contributors often tweaked a few values in a calculation from one of their own recent papers so the new result couldn't be guessed from the old one. According to the researchers, problems like these are often handed to PhD students as a first step into research.

An example from black hole research shows how demanding these problems still are. Solving it means finding an older paper, carrying its equations over from a five-dimensional to a four-dimensional spacetime, and then computing the result with a custom program. Coordinator Suvrat Raju, a co-author of the older paper, needed about a day. The authors estimate that before modern agents arrived, only a handful of experts had both the physics knowledge and the experience with these computational methods. Even they would have needed several days.

The problems span eleven subfields of theoretical physics, from fluid flows and biological processes to particle physics and cosmology. Each agent ran the test twice, once under realistic conditions with web search and once in isolation without internet access.

Anthropic's Opus 5.5, running in Claude Code, came in second at 92 percent. Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash scored 68 percent, while the open-weight models DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM 5.3 reached 54 and 42 percent. The weaker models sometimes made mistakes an expert would have caught right away. On the black hole problem, Gemini and GLM copied the formulas from the older paper unchanged during the web search run. Those formulas apply to five dimensions, not the required four.

Internet access made surprisingly little difference. Without web search, Astra and Opus each scored 92 percent. Many problems depend on formulas from research papers that the models usually didn't receive. The authors take this as a sign that leading language models have effectively memorized large parts of the theoretical physics literature.

With web search, Astra solved everything except one problem that stumped every model. It asked for an equation that produces a given curve. The experts' solution relies on special mathematical forms that only count as the required differential equation in a broader sense. The authors admit the problem might seem "unfair," but they consider it realistic because researchers often have to infer the underlying physics from imprecise data.

## Several AI misses turned out to be flaws in the answer key

For several problems, follow-ups with the experts revealed small, hard-to-spot errors in their reference solutions. Once those were fixed, Astra's answer was correct every time.

This pattern could also explain an apparent contradiction. The agents do better on TheoPhysEval than on some other physics benchmarks, such as CritPt , even though the authors consider their own problems harder on average. A recent study found that some theoretical physics benchmarks are graded incorrectly and in some cases badly underestimate what the models can do.

Anyone who wants to check the results can download the problems and test setup as a dataset on Hugging Face.

## Why strong calculations haven't led to physics breakthroughs

The authors write that some of the strongest current models may already have surpassed the best human researchers on concrete calculations, even in specialized fields. They call this a major milestone.

The impact is even more visible in mathematics, they note, where AI agents have already solved important open problems. According to OpenAI , that includes the Navier-Stokes problem about the equations that describe fluid flow, one of the famous Millennium Prize Problems. Theoretical physics hasn't seen a comparable breakthrough yet.

The authors explain that a concrete calculation with a verifiable result only comes at the end of the research process. Before that, someone has to build a theory and ask it the "right" questions. When a problem turns out to be too hard, a good researcher switches to a related problem that's simpler and just as interesting. Current agents aren't good at that.

Physicists also share a common, if far from unanimous, sense of what makes a problem interesting. Agents don't seem to have this "taste" yet. When asked to design new problems, they get lost in details a human would find boring.

The researchers stress that these observations can't be quantified and aren't a forecast of where AI is headed. They think AI agents could do top-level research on their own in the near future, but that will take more than the ability to solve problems.

## AI is already changing how physicists train and who can compete

The authors already see consequences for training. Until recently, some of the benchmark problems would have worked well as first research projects for early-career researchers. That's no longer appropriate unless the goal is explicitly just to work through the material.

They also point to a structural problem: Theoretical physics has historically needed far less money than experimental research, which has kept opportunities in the field relatively equal. Capable AI agents could change that. The benchmark problems are still cheap to solve, and Astra's full run cost about $116. For harder problems, though, the authors expect resource needs to climb sharply. At that point, a research group's budget could have more say over what it can accomplish, even in theoretical physics. The authors say this raises questions about access and equal opportunity in the field.

Mathematics is already having these debates, for example around the Leiden Declaration . The authors argue theoretical physics should have them too, before AI upends the field. At least one school of thought in physics has so far urged researchers to "shut up and calculate." If taste and vision start to matter more, physicists may need to "stop and think" instead.

# "How much beauty have we lost?" Mathematicians react with shock and disgust as OpenAI bulldozes their field

Mathematicians worldwide are reacting to OpenAI's mass release of hundreds of claimed proofs. More than a hundred researchers have shared their responses, ranging from intellectual fascination to deep grief over a lost way of working.

AI models have long struggled with math. Just a few years ago, they failed at problems that advanced students could solve routinely. But breakthroughs have been piling up since mid-2026 . First came the Unit Distance Conjecture, then Navier-Stokes, then ten solutions presented at the unveiling of OpenAI's Astra model.

OpenAI went much further on October 6, 2026. The company released more than 700 manuscripts at once, claiming solutions to hundreds of open math problems. The math blog Proofs and Prompts then collected over 100 responses from researchers.

## Promising results come with doubts about how they were released

It's too early to fully assess the mathematical substance of what OpenAI uploaded to GitHub . Some papers have already been withdrawn, and others have drawn criticism for being difficult to read. Still, several experts say the results impressed them.

Fields Medalist Peter Scholze urged patience. "We should remember that we are all in this together; mathematics is a marathon, not a sprint; and the goal is and always will be the human understanding of mathematics, which will invariably take time."

Scholze also warned of risks beyond mathematics. He raised the possibility that these systems could find ways to break widely used encryption methods . He wrote that the difficulty of finding such algorithms "does, to my non-expert eyes, not significantly exceed what these systems are now capable of." The consequences for digital infrastructure would be catastrophic.

Terence Tao described mixed feelings about the release. The AI-generated proofs appeared to "introduce clever new ideas that will be fruitful once digested," he wrote. But he was also "deeply frustrated" by the absence of people who could discuss the work, present it in talks, or teach students about it. He mourned the "path not taken" and called for solidarity. "[…] the community needs to come together more than ever."

Alvaro Lozano-Robledo called October 6 "possibly the single most important day in the history of mathematics thus far," while also pointing to the models' limits. OpenAI had targeted the Riemann Hypothesis, mathematics' most famous unsolved conjecture, but managed only a weaker variant. "[…] quasi-RH is huge! But it is not RH."

Some results left Ben Green stunned. He described them as "absolutely shocking to me." According to Green, the release resolved roughly three-quarters of the research goals covered by a prestigious European grant he had received just that June.

Roman Sauer recognized a technique he had developed over years in OpenAI's solutions to two entirely different problems. "I am stunned."

Johannes Schmitt argued that the research papers were a secondary result of OpenAI's efforts to improve its models, rather than an exercise primarily aimed at advancing mathematics. In his view, the company used unsolved problems for testing because frontier models had outgrown easier challenges.

Ian Agol compared the situation with Grigori Perelman's release of one of the century's most important proofs in 2002. The Russian mathematician gave few talks about his work. Agol noted that several research teams then spent years reconstructing the missing steps.

## "[…] a trillion-dollar company showed up and just blasted the whole thing with TNT […]"

Few responses focus on the quality of the solutions themselves. Many mathematicians instead describe shock, paralysis, and fears about their future in the profession.

Hugo Duminil-Copin , a 2022 Fields Medalist, wrote, "I expected that one day we would be surpassed, and that it would happen systematically. But yesterday's announcement hit with a force I had not anticipated."

According to Duminil-Copin, OpenAI claimed results on every major unsolved problem he had publicly discussed over his career. "But not all of them. Not all at once. Not with such nonchalance."

"The shock is immense. I am paralysed." He added, "Tomorrow, we will find a way forward. [...] But for now, I simply don't have the energy."

Matt Zaremsky described four years of steady progress toward a particular problem, with his research program producing a major advance about once a year. In his account, OpenAI stepped in once the problem had gained enough prominence.

"[...] it feels like we've been working on an archeological dig for 4 years, gradually discovering more and more of a really cool-looking dinosaur skeleton, and then a trillion-dollar company showed up and just blasted the whole thing with TNT, handed us the whole skeleton, and walked away." He summed up the experience as "not great."

Tasmin Chu became attached to a probability theory problem as a student. It was what drew her into research. "[...] what I wanted more than to know that pc<pu is true was the time and space to think about it for the next few years."

Chu distinguished between her personal love of mathematical thought, which she said remained hers, and her ability to shape her own professional work. "To be frank, I find myself absolutely disgusted by the society I live in."

For PhD student Tristan Humbert , the announcement threatened both his research plans and his job search. He learned that morning that OpenAI claimed to have proved the problem at the center of his dissertation.

Humbert described sadness followed by panic over his postdoc applications. He spent the morning revising his research plan. Reading the paper turned those feelings into anger when he encountered what he called "mostly unreadable slop."

Enrico Fatighenti said researchers were holding AI-generated papers to a different standard from human work. He would reject a submission if its opening page was too poorly written to follow. Yet, he argued, the community was now being asked to decipher and explain papers from AI systems.

"This comes at a considerable cost to us in terms of time and effort, while they can simply move on and slop-bulldoze the next conjecture. And, of course, the credit remains theirs."

Henry Wilton was more blunt. "If OpenAI wanted to destroy the mathematical community, this would be a great way to go about it."

Wilton criticized OpenAI for withholding authors' names and information about failure rates. He argued that the lack of named authors implied "that mathematics is no longer a human endeavour."

Sam Hughes expressed his feelings in three sentences. "It was a privilege of a lifetime to get to do research level maths. But not like this. How much beauty have we lost?"

Japanese mathematician Koji Fujiwara responded with lyrics set to Dolly Parton's "Jolene."

> "AI, AI, AI, AI I'm begging of you, please don't take my math AI, AI, AI, AI Please don't take it just because you can"

## Researchers disagree on what remains for humans

Some researchers see reasons for optimism. Danny Calegari said personal curiosity had guided his choice of projects for the past 15 years, and OpenAI's release hadn't affected his current work.

Calegari described a collaboration with a musician on a soundtrack for a mathematical animation. Anthropic's Claude had written the code. "If that's not worth celebrating I don't know what is."

Constantin Kogler had been working with Astra on a problem that OpenAI also claimed to have solved. He posted his own paper on arXiv a day after the company's release. "[...] I can't help but feel like living in a mathematical wonderland with the next field-defining idea being discovered whenever I am ready for it."

Giovanni Mongardi saw a much bleaker future. "Today, something is lost forever." He described mathematicians' remaining role as "priests of the Machine-God" and feared "the future of the mind will be a desert, with no questions to guide us beyond the horizon."

Concern for younger researchers runs through nearly all the responses. Mark Hagen said requests for help from distressed early-career colleagues took priority over examining the preprints that day.

Petra Schwer said she and other mathematicians had become more guarded when discussing research. "Mistrust is spreading, and that is not good." Mitchell Taylor said many colleagues were experiencing "severe anxiety, depression and loss of purpose."

Martin Bridson acknowledged both the opportunities and the losses. But he cautioned against letting AI labs set the research agenda. "At the same time, we must resist the temptation to believe that digging insights out of announcements from AI labs will become the paramount task of our time." "We should embrace the power that the machines offer, but we should not be indentured to follow their lead."

## Months of tension have become a personal crisis

The Association for Human Mathematics had already called for a boycott of OpenAI , accusing the company of violating core norms of scientific research. Twenty-five Fields Medalists, including Tao and Scholze, had also issued a joint statement warning of a serious misalignment between the goals of the AI industry and those of mathematics.

Tao had outlined a "Math 2.0" era in which solving problems alone could no longer be the field's central focus. The responses so far show how deeply personal this shift is for mathematicians.

# Inception's Mercury 3 diffusion model claims to beat GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at a fraction of the wait

## Key Points

- AI startup Inception has released Mercury 3, a diffusion-based language model. Instead of writing text word by word, it refines a rough draft of the whole answer step by step. Inception says this makes it much faster than standard models.

- In Inception's internal benchmarks, Mercury 3 generates more than 1,000 tokens per second on Nvidia GPUs. It leads rivals like GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 in eight of 12 tests.

- The model can process up to 1 million tokens at once and uses an OpenAI-compatible API. Inception built it mainly for real-time apps where speed matters, like autonomous AI agents, smart glasses, and customer support.

Inception says its new language model, Mercury 3, beats GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on a range of benchmarks while running four to eight times faster.

In its announcement , the company calls Mercury 3 the most capable diffusion language model released so far.

The speed comes from how the model is built. Models like GPT or Claude write one word at a time, so each new word has to wait for the one before it. Diffusion models are best known from image generation. They first sketch a rough version of the whole answer and then refine it over several passes, generating many words at once. Google's technical report on DiffusionGemma explains the basic idea. Ad

## Mercury 3's lead is narrower than the announcement suggests

Inception's own benchmark table tells a more mixed story. Mercury 3 wins eight of 12 tests, with all three models running at medium settings. The gap is widest in instruction following. On IFBench, Mercury 3 scores 76.84 points, 15 more than GPT-6 Luna. It also leads clearly in autonomous coding on SWE-Bench Atlas with 51.08 points, while its rivals reach 33.33 and 32.26. Ad

Claude Haiku 5.5 wins the longer coding test DeepSWE. It's also better at finding information in long texts. GPT-6 Luna edges ahead in two tests from Artificial Analysis. Inception's short overview is more cautious, describing Mercury 3's quality as on par or better.

According to Inception, Mercury 3 generates 1,068 tokens per second on Nvidia GPUs. In the company's comparison, Claude Haiku 5.5 manages about 240 and GPT-6 Luna about 130. No independent tests exist yet. Ad

Inception says Mercury 3 has more than 40 times as many parameters as Mercury 1 but runs just as fast. Performance has also tripled since the small Mercury 1 mini. Inception sees this as a sign that diffusion models reliably improve as they scale, just like standard language models. The exact parameter count remains undisclosed.

## Mercury 3 targets apps where small delays add up

Inception is pitching Mercury 3 mainly for AI agents, search, customer support, and tutoring. AI agents complete tasks in many separate steps and wait on the model at each one. Those small delays pile up fast. Ad

Early-access partners share their results in the announcement, and most of them also focus on speed. Octen AI builds search features for smart glasses. "On smart glasses, an answer that takes five seconds feels broken," says founder Kuan Zou. He says the search itself took only about 80 milliseconds, and the language model was the bottleneck. With Mercury 3, the median response arrived after 0.9 seconds. The full process took 2.2 seconds. Ad

Education company General Learning says it now delivers hints and corrections to students in about one second. Customer service provider Lorikeet reports faster response times along with better results. At TinyFish AI, co-founder Shuhao Zhang says Mercury 3 was given 50 navigation tasks on real websites. It solved 25, beating GPT-6.1-Sol. Zhang doesn't give a number for the OpenAI model.

## Mercury 3's low launch pricing may not last

Regular pricing is $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.70 per million output tokens. Inception is cutting prices in half at launch. It hasn't said when the discount ends. After that, Mercury 3 would cost more for output than GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, at least for shorter inputs, where both charge $0.50. For very long prompts, though, both rivals charge a lot more. Mercury 3 can handle up to 1 million tokens at once.

The model is available on Inception's own platform as well as OpenRouter, Baseten, and Vercel. It uses the same API as OpenAI's models, so Inception says developers can switch with little effort.

In February, Inception released Mercury 2 , which it called the first diffusion model to reason through intermediate steps before answering. Before that, the startup raised $50 million . Backers include NVentures, M12, and Snowflake Ventures, the venture arms of Nvidia, Microsoft, and Snowflake.

Google is working on the same approach. Its Gemini Diffusion demo was followed in June by the open model DiffusionGemma . Google says it runs up to four times faster than the standard Gemma 4 but delivers slightly weaker results.

# Is AI interpretability close to a breakthrough? A new essay has researchers divided

Neural networks aren't nearly as tangled as researchers assumed, according to Nick Cammarata, one of the people behind the superposition hypothesis. OpenAI's Roon calls it a historic moment. Google DeepMind researcher Neel Nanda warns against overhyping it.

In a long essay titled "Neural Networks Are Already Clean," Nick Cammarata argues that the inner workings of large AI models are much easier to understand than previously thought. Cammarata is a researcher at the interpretability lab Goodfire. With the essay, he rejects an explanation he helped shape years ago.

Mechanistic interpretability tries to do more than watch what an AI model outputs. It aims to trace how the model arrives at its answers internally. Ideally, each of the millions of artificial neurons would stand for a recognizable concept. In practice, many neurons seemed to fire on completely unrelated things, which researchers call polysemanticity. One early and famous example is a neuron in the image model InceptionV1 that responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. Cammarata used it as an example in his own early research.

The standard explanation was superposition. The theory goes that when a network runs out of neurons, it packs unrelated concepts into the same neurons because they rarely get in each other's way. The result looks like a knot. That's why many labs train a second model, such as a sparse autoencoder, to pull the concepts apart. They then study that model instead of the original.

Cammarata played a major role in shaping this view. With Chris Olah, he co-wrote the paper "Zoom In" , which introduced the first superposition circuit. In 2023, he started an automated interpretability project at OpenAI. At the time, only about 1.7 percent of neurons counted as understandable, even by the most generous measure.

## The evidence may have been misread

Cammarata now thinks the most famous examples were misinterpreted. He says the cat-car neuron is really a V-shape detector. Pointed shapes like fox snouts or flames activate it, while round shapes like the letter O push its activation negative. So it doesn't represent two completely unrelated concepts like cat faces and cars, which means it isn't an example of superposition.

He also reinterprets the superposition circuit from "Zoom In," where a car seemed to hide among dog neurons. In his view, it's ordinary generalization, and the circuit simply groups cars and dogs by which way they face the camera. He blames the mess in InceptionV1's late layers on an outdated architecture and weak analysis tools.

Cammarata explains the remaining ambiguity with a pattern he calls "recursive generalization." He says a neuron grows like a branch that sprouts side shoots. One neuron that recognized the letter sequence "iy" later responded to "diy" and eventually to "do it yourself," which doesn't contain "iy" at all. Unlike superposition, these groupings can teach you something about the network.

For language models, he offers preliminary numbers. In Qwen3-32B, about 90 percent of neuron poles have one main job and about 7 percent have two related ones. Only 2 to 4 percent remain unexplained. Goodfire says it sees similar results in models with up to trillions of parameters. AI agents that analyze neurons in bulk did most of the work. Cammarata borrows from Rich Sutton's "Bitter Lesson" and concludes that in interpretability, too, simple investigation at massive scale beats clever decomposition methods.

Cammarata doesn't introduce a fundamentally new method. He goes back to the field's original approach of studying neurons directly, just with better tools, larger models, and automated agents.

## Readable networks would be a big win for AI safety

If Cammarata is right, that would be good news, especially for AI safety. Right now, apart from monitoring chains of thought that keep getting less reliable , there are few ways to tell whether a model is deceiving people or behaving dangerously. Cammarata doubts that alignment, the work of steering AI toward human goals, can be solved without interpretability, because otherwise we don't know what we're building. Deception has no reason to hide from the model's own circuits, he writes. If humans become just another "reader" of the network, they can see the deception too, and errors might be fixed in a targeted way.

Roon, an OpenAI employee who posts under that pseudonym on X and is an influential voice in AI circles, was thrilled. He says he's close friends with Cammarata and would never have ended up at OpenAI without him. The work "may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history," Roon wrote . He added that the news is so good even Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the most prominent voices warning of an AI catastrophe, will have to lower his estimated odds of doom. In Roon's view, alignment could become a "normal science."

Even Roon has some reservations. Others in the field still need to confirm the results and he also suspects that interpretability breakthroughs will push AI capabilities forward. The fact that they're coming from outside doesn't bode well for the big labs, OpenAI included.

## Nanda sees a useful tool, not a breakthrough

Neel Nanda is far more measured. He's considered one of the founding figures of mechanistic interpretability and leads the interpretability team at Google DeepMind. Before that, he worked at Anthropic and as an independent researcher. His views have shifted, according to him: Since mid-2024, he's grown more pessimistic about ambitious interpretability and has leaned toward pragmatic approaches. His team deprioritized research on sparse autoencoders. They didn't think the technique was useless, but it didn't seem worth the effort the field was putting into it.

Cammarata's work is interesting but doesn't really change the big picture, Nanda writes . Neuron-based analysis could help with practical questions, like why a model did something questionable, and it's much easier to apply to frontier models. But he doesn't buy the idea that interpretability is close to being fully cracked. He expects neuron-based analysis to have serious flaws and miss a lot as well.

Nanda still thinks superposition is real. He argues that language models store far more facts than they have neurons, and weak activations in particular likely hold much of that information. He doubts that findings from small image models carry over. He also thinks the essay defines monosemanticity too loosely but does give Cammarata credit for checking his old work with modern tools.

Part of the dispute comes down to definitions: Cammarata has no problem with models representing more concepts than they have dimensions, and Nanda sees him as agreeing on that point. What Cammarata disputes is that networks arbitrarily pack completely unrelated things together.

The technical companion paper hasn't been released yet. As an interpretability company, Goodfire also has an obvious stake in the thesis. If Cammarata's reading holds up, he thinks automated researchers could do in months what took humans nearly a decade with image models. He writes that there may not be much time left for that.

# Machine learning pioneer Michael I. Jordan dismantles AI doom rhetoric as "grand moralizing performance"

Michael I. Jordan, described by Science in 2016 as "the most influential computer scientist," calls warnings about existential AI threats pure science fiction. In a wide-ranging interview, he takes aim at doomers, company founders, and naive junior researchers.

Jordan, professor emeritus at UC Berkeley, pushed back hard against AI doom rhetoric in an interview with Libération . The 70-year-old machine learning pioneer now works full-time at Inria, the French National Institute for Research in Digital Science and Technology in Paris, where he heads the new "markets and learning" chair. When asked about the summer's AI discourse, he called it "totally frustrating."

Jordan warned about the reckless overuse of the term AI back in 2019 . "I wasn't the only one saying it. It was obvious that it would create the hysteria we're seeing now," he says. "You've seen what happened: AI wasn't enough, so they started talking about AGI, and now it's 'superintelligence'..." Ad

## Resignations as "moralizing performance"

Jordan dismisses AI companies' demands for regulation as "theater," a way of saying "Look, we're the good guys" while they "would like to have total control over how they are regulated." Ad

The resignation of young Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon , which sparked a wave of collective hysteria over an "AIpocalypse" scenario in early September, is a textbook example in Jordan's view. Many young employees at these companies "aren't really engineers," he says. "They come from the humanities, philosophy, or other disciplines. They're 25 years old, they're naive, they don't do engineering work, they've never worked at large companies where real products are developed for real people, with discipline."

They "get together, a bit like in Parisian cafés in the 1920s, to talk about these grand science-fiction ideas." When they resign, they know they're going to attract attention. "It allows them to feel virtuous and to be seen as very important figures. They claim to be giving up money, but in reality, they already have their stock options." Jordan sees the whole thing as "a grand moralizing performance that doesn't serve the real objective it claims to pursue. There's a great deal of naiveté here, which goes hand in hand with a certain cynicism..." Ad

## Superintelligence belongs in science fiction

"Superintelligence" is "a science-fiction term," Jordan says, "and a large part of the debates I've witnessed belong to the realm of science fiction." Occasionally discussing far-fetched scenarios is fine. "Talking about it behind the scenes, as a science-fiction topic, is fine. But when it becomes the dominant discourse, it's very, very harmful. For technological development, for young people, and for the mindset of countries alike." The term is currently being pushed on the US tech elite by President Trump, who are happy to play along .

Jordan is especially harsh on Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, who has a track record of making bold claims that don't always hold up . "Geoffrey Hinton has never created a company that offers real services for real people," he says. "Hinton believes that we have figured out how the brain works and that we can reproduce it in silicon; we would therefore be able to copy it as many times as we wanted and, by combining what all these copies learn, we would obtain a kind of exponential growth and, there you have it: superintelligence. None of the steps in this argument is credible. Here, we're in the land of science fiction." Ad

He's slightly more generous toward Yoshua Bengio . "Yoshua is a little different; he takes action and does things that directly focus on safety." Bengio's warnings tend to target shortcomings in current AI technology, such as agent swarms spiraling out of control . Ad

Jordan frames the hack of Hugging Face by OpenAI agents as bad engineering. "In chemical engineering, we would never have had a situation where explosions were allowed to happen just to see how badly things could go wrong." OpenAI was "conducting rather stupid experiments, letting the agents do whatever they wanted and encouraging this behavior." The doomers then loved turning it into something scary. "My God, these agents are self-aware and are trying to find a way to destroy humans." That, too, is science fiction, according to Jordan.

## The trillion-dollar bet on data centers

Jordan considers the massive data center investments "just an enormous bet, but we have absolutely no idea whether it will pay off." LLMs are already capable enough for natural language tasks, and trillions spent on data centers won't necessarily deliver much more . "Instead, we often will want to add a bit of specialized knowledge in a particular field based on local knowledge. But you don't need a gigantic data center to do that. Particularly if you use open-weight models that you integrate into your company."

# Mathematicians say OpenAI doesn't understand its own Navier-Stokes proof

In early September, the company presented a 166-page potential solution to the Navier-Stokes problem. OpenAI claimed the proof followed the approach of Spanish mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa.

Several groups of experts now disagree, Scientific American reports . "When you go to the details, it is a different approach," says mathematician Gonzalo Cao-Labora of EPFL. The similarities are only surface-level, he says.

The potential proof is written in Lean, a formal verification language that checks every logical step but doesn't make it readable to humans on its own. The Clay Mathematics Institute (CMI) has been reviewing it since its release. Ad

Before publication, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster accused OpenAI of building on work that he and Anthropic's Levent Alpöge had done with publicly available models. OpenAI denied the claim, saying it never used Buckmaster's data. A definitive answer is probably impossible because language models are black boxes, according to Camillo De Lellis of the Institute for Advanced Study. Ad

In early October, OpenAI dumped roughly 400 more results that the math community can barely keep up with. Publishing them as a loose collection on GitHub angered many mathematicians , who felt it cheapened their field.

# NASA and IBM's open source lunar model turns 17 years of orbiter data into a foundation for lunar science

The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model makes decades of lunar observation data usable for machine learning. It's especially strong at predicting ice deposits at the poles and detecting craters.

"NASA has spent decades building an extraordinary scientific record of the Moon, but collecting data is only part of the job," says Kevin Murphy, NASA's chief science data officer. The data also has to be easier for scientists to use, he adds. NASA and IBM Research, working with several academic institutions, have now released the NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model. The two organizations describe it as one of the first open-source foundation models for lunar science.

Unlike task-specific algorithms, a foundation model is pretrained on large volumes of unlabeled data and can then be adapted to specific tasks with just a few labeled examples. The team sees this as the main benefit for lunar research, where observation data is plentiful but labels are scarce. Ad

## Nearly 2 million tile bundles from 17 years of observation

The team trained the model from scratch using SomBench, which they say is the largest co-registered multimodal lunar corpus to date. It contains nearly 2 million tile bundles across 11 modalities and two spatial scales. About 1 million high-resolution images come from the Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) at roughly 1 meter per pixel, while just under 964,000 multispectral images come from the Wide Angle Camera at 100 meters per pixel. Ad

The bulk of the data comes from 17 years of observations by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). According to NASA, its data volume exceeds that of all other NASA planetary missions combined. Data from the GRAIL mission (gravity field), Lunar Prospector (hydrogen), and JAXA's Kaguya/SELENE probe (mineralogy) rounded out the collection.

In total, the dataset brings together more than 30 spatially aligned data layers from nine instruments and four missions. To prevent leakage between training, validation, and test data, the corpus is split geographically by map zones rather than randomly distributing individual tiles. Ad

## The model gets lighting conditions as input instead of guessing them

The model is based on TerraMind , a multimodal Earth observation model, but the researchers trained it from scratch instead of fine-tuning it. For each tile, the model receives the imaging geometry as explicit context, including illumination angles, sun position, and tile extent. On the Moon, lighting geometry shapes how the surface looks far more than the surface's actual properties do. Rather than forcing the model to correct for this from raw pixels, the team simply feeds it that information.

The model also learns from high-resolution and coarse imagery together in a single training run, capturing both fine details and large-scale context. A technique called FlexiViT lets the same trained model adapt to tasks with different image patch sizes without retraining. Ad

## Ice prediction is where the model pulls ahead most

The team tested the model on crater detection at 100-meter and 1-meter scales and on predicting polar ice deposits. It also had to segment Irregular Mare Patches (IMPs), young volcanic features that challenge established timelines of lunar cooling. Across all tasks, the pretrained model matched or beat both common baselines and an architecturally identical control model with random initialization, according to the technical report . Ad

The biggest gains showed up in ice deposit prediction. Permanently shadowed polar regions stay cold enough to preserve water ice for billions of years and are considered a potential resource for water, oxygen, and rocket fuel. The model cut prediction error by up to 22 percent compared to the best baseline, SwinV2-B, according to IBM.

For coarse-scale crater detection, the model beat SwinV2-B by nearly 19 percent, according to IBM. That number comes from training with only half the data, suggesting the model needs fewer labeled examples to perform well.

## Part of the edge comes from how the model handles data

Even the randomly initialized control model beat five of seven baselines on ice prediction without any lunar pretraining. According to the researchers, part of the advantage comes from how the model handles different data types. It assigns each data layer its own processing path, while baseline models treat all inputs as stacked channels.

On meter-scale crater detection and IMP segmentation, the model roughly ties the strongest baselines, with differences falling within the variance between training runs. IBM claims a 3 percent lead over SwinV2-B on IMPs, but the results look more comparable than clearly better.

According to the researchers, LoRA, a lighter fine-tuning method that trains only a fraction of the parameters, kept pace with full fine-tuning across the board and did better on crater detection. Full fine-tuning only wins on the two smallest tasks.

## Useful for analysis, but no substitute for physical measurements

Juan Bernabé-Moreno, director of IBM Research Europe, said the model connects observations across instruments and reveals patterns that are difficult to spot in isolation.

The model isn't suited for absolute geodetic positioning, the research shows. In generation tests, latitude and longitude were off by dozens of degrees in some cases, and elevation structures could appear with shifted absolute height values even when their shapes were reconstructed correctly.

The authors see it as a reusable foundation for downstream tasks, not a replacement for physical measurement instruments. Controlled experiments isolating the contribution of each innovation are still pending, and some test datasets are small.

## Part of a growing model family

The model is publicly available on Hugging Face , the code is on GitHub , and it's integrated into the open-source toolkit TerraTorch. The team also released the ML-ready pretraining datasets and benchmark collections.

The model is part of the NASA-IBM "AI for Science" collaboration. Both organizations have been working on foundation models under a Space Act Agreement since early 2022. In August 2023, they released the first Prithvi model on Hugging Face , trained on Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery of the entire contiguous US and adapted for flood and wildfire mapping.

IBM had announced Prithvi as part of its Watsonx platform . IBM developed TerraMind, the lunar model's base, in 2025 with ESA and Forschungszentrum Jülich for Earth observation.

Google Deepmind is pursuing a related approach with AlphaEarth Foundations , compressing optical satellite imagery, radar, lidar scans, and climate simulations into compact embeddings of Earth's surface.

# Nvidia open-sources Flora to make robot video labeling 125x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra

Labeling one hour of robot video for 72 cents instead of $88 is what Nvidia promises with Flora, its open data engine. But the comparison with GPT-6 Astra isn't quite as lopsided as the price tag suggests.

Large AI models for robots learn from videos that need text annotations, and according to Nvidia's GEAR research lab, this requires three types of labels. First, descriptions of what action happens when in the video, used to select training data. Second, ratings of how well a robot progresses step by step, so it can learn through trial and error. And third, judgments on whether a task was completed successfully, used to monitor robots during deployment. Most existing tools only provide one of these types. Large language models like GPT-6 Astra can generate several, but they're too expensive for the massive volumes of video involved.

According to the paper , Flora covers all three. Nvidia says the system is already running during training of its GR00T models, annotating up to 200,000 hours of video per day across 512 GB300 GPUs. The models are available on Hugging Face .

Flora consists of three fine-tuned Qwen3.5 models . A 9B model splits videos into action segments, and a 27B model describes them while factoring in what happened before and after each action. A second 27B model called Flora-Rewarder takes on three roles depending on the prompt. It rates an episode's success on a scale of 1 to 5, classifies each half-second step as normal, suboptimal, or failure, and assigns scores based on self-defined rubrics.

## Up to 125x cheaper by Nvidia's own estimates

In a test with 50 videos, Flora scored slightly better than GPT-6 Astra according to Nvidia, even though OpenAI's model was allowed to use its full reasoning capacity. Labeling one hour of video runs about 72 cents with Flora by Nvidia's estimate, compared to roughly $88.50 with GPT-6 Astra. Claude Opus 5 scored much worse in the same test and still cost about $42 per hour.

The Flora cost figures are projections, though, not production measurements. Nvidia calculated them based on an assumed rental price of $10 per GPU per hour.

## Flora finds actions better, but Astra often describes them more precisely

On the public WGO-Bench, Flora is best at detecting action boundaries but trails Astra in overall score and falls behind Gemini 3.8 Flash in pure description accuracy. According to the researchers, the gains come mainly from temporal localization.

On Nvidia's own DenseCaptionBench, Flora leads across all metrics for human recordings, but for robot videos the model comes in second behind Astra. There's a methodological catch the researchers acknowledge, too. GPT-6 Astra evaluates the descriptions while also being one of the models under test.

## Almost no other model catches mid-episode errors

On RoboRewardBench, Flora's error rate is 27.8 percent lower than Astra's. The paper attributes the gap to partially completed tasks. When a robot only tips a bottle over instead of knocking it off the table, Flora assigns 3 out of 5 points to match the human reference, while Astra gives just one.

Flora-Rewarder catches 53.3 percent of failed steps within an episode, while no competitor gets above 11.7 percent and Astra doesn't catch a single one. The tradeoff is that Flora falsely flags about 11 percent of normal steps as errors. Astra still leads on rubric-based scoring and trajectory ranking.

In a video with many short hand movements, Flora identifies 34 of 37 individual actions, while Astra catches only four. On the flip side, Flora sometimes splits longer actions into too many small steps and occasionally gets descriptions wrong. In one video, a robot hand wipes a plate with a cloth, but Flora describes it as folding a napkin.

Nvidia positions Flora as an open alternative to commercial services like Scale AI's Physical AI Data Engine. Researchers can use it to scale their own robotics datasets and test approaches like transferring human demonstrations to robots. Nvidia is investing billions in open AI models to keep developers in its hardware ecosystem and drive demand for its chips, and Flora serves that same goal.

The company has also been working for some time to offset the shortage of robotics training data through simulation and automated data processing . At GTC earlier this year, Nvidia showed a data pipeline that automatically prepares, multiplies, and scores training material. Flora adds detailed labels and reward signals from video to that pipeline.

All of this feeds into Nvidia's strategy of covering the entire robotics value chain , from hardware and training data to simulation and the AI models themselves. Google's recently announced Gemini 4 Argon targets a similar part of the robotics training process, also identifying work steps in training videos and flagging failed actions.
