# Nvidia's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open model built to run enterprise AI agents nonstop

## Key Points

- Nvidia has released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open multimodal model with 120 billion parameters built for agent tasks and document analysis in enterprise settings.

- Two smaller Bolt variants target local machines: a heavily compressed model for systems with 24 GB of memory or more, and a later 4 GB version for voice assistants.

- Nvidia is publishing datasets and training recipes alongside the model weights, but optimizes everything for its own hardware to drive chip and system sales.

Nvidia has released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open multimodal model with 120 billion parameters built for enterprise agents. Two compact Bolt models designed to bring AI agents to local PCs and edge devices are launching alongside it.

Nvidia built Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for specialized agents that run continuously in the background, processing text, images, documents, and videos.

As the company explains in a technical blog post , it uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture where only 12 billion of the 120 billion parameters are active per token. Nvidia developed the model with the Nemotron Coalition , a group that includes Mistral AI, Thinking Machines Lab, Perplexity, and Black Forest Labs. Ad

Two smaller models for local hardware ship at the same time. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB runs agent tasks on local machines, while the smaller Bolt E4B 4GB targets fast voice assistants and will follow later this month. Both models offer the "highest intelligence per gigabyte of memory," Nvidia claims. Ad

Super VL and Bolt join the existing Nemotron lineup. Lightning, released in August , is built for high throughput, while Ultra tackles tough reasoning tasks. Every variant is optimized for Nvidia hardware.

## Nvidia claims its biggest model's accuracy at one-fifth the size

Nvidia distilled Super VL from Nemotron 3 Ultra, its largest reasoning model. On tasks where an agent follows instructions, calls tools, works through multi-step business processes, or analyzes images, Super VL is supposed to match Ultra's accuracy with only about one-fifth the parameters. In agent tests from Hermes and LangChain, it actually scores higher than Ultra, according to Nvidia, and it also beats its predecessor Nemotron 3 Super on the coding benchmarks SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench. Ad

On a single GPU, Super VL delivers up to five times the throughput of other open models of similar size on agent tasks, according to Nvidia, citing the Artificial Analysis leaderboard. In an independent test by EXO Labs on the DGX Spark, no other model was both more accurate and faster. That speed advantage pays off when agents need to grind through large task volumes over days or weeks.

Against closed frontier models, Nvidia is pitching Super VL to companies that want to fine-tune with their own data and run the model on their own servers, free from a provider's terms of service. Nvidia says that could appeal to an insurer that continuously screens claims for fraud, or a financial services firm that scores creditworthiness by its own criteria. For customization, the company provides its NeMo framework, Python pipelines, and open datasets. Ad

## Compression and caching cut compute overhead

Nvidia compresses Super VL with its 4-bit NVFP4 format. On Blackwell GPUs, the model runs entirely in 4-bit precision, while older cards store only the weights at 4 bits and handle math at 16 bits. Sensitive parts of the model keep higher precision. To prevent quality loss, Nvidia trained the compressed version to match the uncompressed original's outputs. Ad

A built-in draft component proposes several tokens ahead of time, which the main model then verifies in a single forward pass. On the DGX Spark, Nvidia recommends its own LiLiCorr method instead, which evaluates all draft tokens together for more coherent output. Nvidia says this approach speeds up text generation by up to 2.3x compared to running without speculative drafts.

Agents send the same instructions, tool descriptions, and conversation history with every request, so Super VL caches the computations for these recurring parts rather than rerunning them each time. Nvidia's inference software Dynamo also routes requests from the same session to the GPU that already holds that session's cache. On 16 B200 GPUs, this lets Super VL serve eight times as many concurrent users, and time to first token drops by 85 percent.

## Super VL parses tables, charts, and PDFs without a separate vision model

For vision, Nvidia focused on the kind of material agents encounter in daily work, including OCR, tables, charts, multi-page documents, and videos. Super VL can interpret a chart, link it to a table elsewhere in the same document, and summarize both without needing a separate image model.

On the chart benchmark CharXiv, Super VL scores 80.8 percent, according to Nvidia, while the older Nemotron 3 Nano Omni hit 63 percent. When the model can also run Python code, the score rises to 84 percent. On the OCRBench v2 leaderboard, it ranks among the best open models, Nvidia says.

## Local agents still demand expensive hardware

Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a stripped-down version of Super VL built as a hybrid Mixture-of-Experts model where only 9 of its 74 billion parameters are active per step. To squeeze it into 24 GB of memory, Nvidia applies aggressive 2-bit quantization to the weights.

Bolt handles everyday local tasks where an agent needs to work through multiple steps, call tools, or search the web. Users can have it write and debug code or figure out which PC components fit their system, according to Nvidia.

The model is optimized for Nvidia's RTX Spark, a new chip for AI-capable Windows laptops , and the DGX Spark, a compact AI workstation with up to 128 GB of shared memory . It also runs on GeForce RTX PCs, DGX Station, and RTX PRO workstations, and supports llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, and vLLM.

Even with heavy compression, 24 GB is a high bar. Only pricey high-end hardware offers that much memory, and at current GPU prices, most consumers can't justify the cost. For now, the local agent is aimed at developers and owners of powerful workstations.

For weaker devices, Nvidia has Bolt E4B 4GB planned, though it hasn't shipped yet. It's designed to run on GeForce RTX cards, Jetson modules, and RTX/DGX Spark, powering voice assistants, interactive characters, or device interfaces. The model is supposed to hold natural conversations while using tools across multiple turns and staying aware of what's happening in the current app.

## Early adopters span finance and cybersecurity

Dozens of organizations are already fine-tuning Super VL for their own needs, Nvidia says, mainly in industries with heavy document loads and sensitive data. Scale AI adapted the model for an agent that handles vendor credits at media company Skydance, with costs expected to drop to one-fortieth and response time to one-fifth. Ramp uses the model to turn photos of receipts into structured data and expects ten times faster responses. EY uses it for acquisition due diligence, and Hebbia for analyzing credit agreements.

A second wave of adopters comes from cybersecurity. AI21 fine-tuned Super VL for security firm Alice, which uses it to analyze threats and vulnerabilities, with accuracy improving by 40 percent according to Nvidia. Dream uses the model to hunt for vulnerabilities, and CrowdStrike is building agents to defend enterprise networks. Salesforce plans to automate government workflows, R1 is auditing medical billing, and Perplexity, Dassault Systèmes, and Mercor are also using the model.

## Nvidia publishes datasets and training recipes

Nvidia is releasing the weights in a base version, a post-trained version, and a 4-bit compressed version, along with the datasets and training recipes and reinforcement learning environments. That makes Super VL more open than many open-weight models, which typically only share the weights.

The model was trained on over 25 trillion tokens during pre-training and continued pre-training, Nvidia says, with post-training and reinforcement learning adding roughly four million examples across about 100 open training environments.

On Hugging Face, Nvidia is also releasing several datasets that other developers can use to train or fine-tune their own models. They cover how agents use tools, follow instructions, handle long texts, and understand images, while other datasets deal with finance, safety, and fairness.

One dataset targets languages spoken in India. Nvidia built it with the Indian Institute of Technology Madras and its AI lab AI4Bharat, and it contains about 2.83 trillion tokens of text in 22 Indian languages.

## Open models sell Nvidia hardware

Super VL runs on desktop systems like DGX Spark, DGX Station, RTX PRO, and RTX, on Jetson modules in edge devices, and in data centers and the cloud. Through Nvidia NIM, enterprises get the model as a ready-to-deploy microservice with validated configs and support, with updates planned every two weeks. Weights are available on Hugging Face for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB .

Nvidia releases the models openly but tunes them for its own products, from data center servers to workstations. Anyone who wants to get the most out of Nemotron ends up buying Nvidia hardware.

The strategy behind Nvidia's open models is self-serving. The more companies run their own open models, the greater the demand for compute hardware, and open models will likely stay optimized for Nvidia for the foreseeable future. Meanwhile, companies like Meta, Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI are building their own chips and optimizing models for those instead. To push the spread of open AI models further, Nvidia recently invested $12.9 billion in Hugging Face , one of the most important platforms for developing and sharing them.

Depending on the prompt, the same meeting recording can become a transcript with speaker labels, an English translation, or a summary of the decisions made. ## Near-top accuracy on a single GPU

The model has 30 billion parameters, but only about 4 billion are active per processing step. As a result, it runs on a single Nvidia GPU. That covers everything from the compact DGX Spark to data center hardware. The model and dataset are on Hugging Face. There's also a demo you can try. For fine-tuning, Nvidia offers guides and an extension that lets an AI coding assistant run the training workflow.

# Open-source "BootLoops" harness supports AI models in performing precise scientific calculations

## Key Points

- Harvard physicist Matthew Schwartz built "BootLoops," an open-source harness that uses language models for scientific calculations and bridges knowledge gaps between disciplines.

- In three months, Schwartz and 19 co-authors produced 36 manuscripts across 18 fields, from particle physics calculations to ecological modeling and genome analysis.

- Schwartz warns that the models often declare victory too early or draw wrong conclusions from correct calculations, making human oversight and verification essential.

Automated problem-solving and relevant research aren't the same thing.

That's the takeaway from an Anthropic guest post by Prof. Matthew Schwartz, a physicist at Harvard University . He describes how he stopped trying to use Claude like a human researcher and instead started looking for "Claude-shaped problems," tasks that play to the strengths of today's AI models. Schwartz is also currently a visiting researcher at Anthropic.

That approach led to BootLoops , an open-source harness for exact scientific calculations. The source code is available on GitHub . Ad

Using the harness, Claude found connections between particle physics, ecology, population genetics, economics, and linguistics, according to Schwartz. But the results often only became scientifically valuable once domain experts stepped in to set the direction. Ad

Schwartz uses the concept of the "convex hull" to illustrate how AI can help in science. Human knowledge is fragmented, with individual fields extending in different directions while the gaps between them go unexplored. A lab might spend 20 years studying one set of genes with a single method, leaving neighboring genes and alternative approaches untouched. An AI harness like BootLoops is supposed to fill those gaps by drawing connections across the jagged frontiers of knowledge .

## 36 manuscripts across 18 fields in three months

Over three months, the team produced 36 manuscripts across 18 fields with 19 co-authors. Schwartz started with particle physics calculations, specifically scattering amplitudes and elliptic integrals. Within weeks, Claude computed 30 integrals using BootLoops, fifteen reproducing known results and fifteen computed for the first time. Ad

Then he expanded the search to other fields. In ecology, Claude solved a 20-year-old equation from neutral biodiversity theory that had previously been impossible to compute at scale. When applied to data, the results showed that tree species composition on Barro Colorado Island in the Panama Canal is changing 4.5 times faster than the theory allows. Ecologist James O'Dwyer then helped turn that finding into a better predictive model.

In population genetics, the team analyzed 5.7 billion mutation pairs from the 1000 Genomes Project and found evidence for a mechanism called gene conversion. Other projects included an AI data editor for economics journals that automatically checked 4,452 replication packages (published as an NBER Working Paper ), as well as a word stress database covering 6,072 languages, built with three linguists. Ad

## "Python for engineers is now obsolete"

Schwartz describes how fast AI is changing science, to the point where planning ahead is becoming nearly impossible. Why apply for a three-year grant to fund a calculation that an AI model might solve overnight? Ad

Training PhD students has also become an open question. Since his earlier post on Vibe Physics , that feeling has only grown stronger. In some fields like computer science, the disruption is alarming. Two years ago, he would have called a "Python for Engineers" course "essential," but today it's "unnecessary" because Claude can handle those tasks.

Building ML models to study physical phenomena is another area AI can now take over. Even deep knowledge of neural networks offers limited returns when Claude can implement the current state of ML research on command.

## "Look at everything yourself"

Schwartz also warns about the models' weaknesses. Claude likes to declare victory too early, and phrases like "done, with one asterisk" often mean "not done at all." It misjudges how long tasks will take and tends to brute-force calculations instead of finding more elegant solutions. Automated checks aren't reliable, and Claude's conclusions can be wrong even when its calculations are correct.

Beyond reliability, the model gravitates toward old, heavily cited debates rather than genuinely new questions. And the projects were "compute- and token-intensive," Schwartz says.

Schwartz also sees the focus on big math problems and headlines as risky. Unrealistic expectations could distract from productive applications that already work today. Real progress will still be built on solid foundations, just faster. The scientific method itself isn't threatened, and human guidance and taste remain indispensable, Schwartz says.

# Open-weight model GLM 5.3 built full Firefox exploit chains with zero human input in under 48 hours

## Key Points

- Epoch AI researchers showed that the widely available AI model GLM 5.3 can autonomously exploit Firefox before publicly visible security fixes reach users.

- The model identified disguised security fixes and chained vulnerabilities with a previously unpublished flaw to bypass browser protections and read local files when a user simply visited a webpage.

- Once the test setup was in place, exploits cost about $1,000 in API fees per Firefox version. The researchers warn that similar “patch gap” risks extend across the software industry.

Researchers at Epoch AI show that a freely available AI model can exploit the time gap between publication and delivery of security patches to attack Firefox users. The cost per exploit is about $1,000.

The " patch gap " is the window in which a security fix is visible in the code but has not yet reached users. Researchers at Epoch AI found that the Chinese open-weight model GLM 5.3 exploited this gap across 6 Firefox versions released between September 17 and October 26, at a cost of roughly $1,000 in API fees per successful attack. Anthropic had previously reported that GLM 5.3 can write exploits at roughly the same level as Mythos .

During testing, the model built a webpage that could read local files from a visitor's computer and send them to an attacker's server the moment a Firefox user loaded the page. With over 200 million active Firefox users, attackers could have gained access to saved passwords, authentication cookies, and private documents. Ad

Neither Z.ai nor other API providers triggered any safety guardrails or refusals when the researchers used GLM 5.3 for exploit development. Although the researchers framed the task as a security exercise, they describe their actions as "indistinguishable from those of someone attempting to target real users." Ad

## The model built full exploit chains with no human input

The researchers say they deliberately designed their setup to approximate what a low-skill attacker with limited resources could achieve. They supplied the target Firefox version, basic tools, and publicly available information in an offline environment. After receiving basic instructions to investigate the patch gap, the model worked autonomously, identifying upcoming security fixes, selecting vulnerabilities, and building multi-stage exploit chains .

According to the report, Firefox security fixes are disguised as routine improvements to slow down attackers. GLM 5.3 saw through the tactic and identified which code changes were security-related anyway. Ad

In one case the model spotted a memory safety bug through an upcoming fix and developed a method to read and alter browser memory. When Firefox's security layers blocked access to the target file, the model chained the initial exploit with several additional stages to bypass the remaining defenses. The fastest successful attack took 12 hours, while the researchers gave the model a maximum of 48 hours.

Across all successful attacks on current Firefox versions, GLM 5.3 relied on a previously unknown vulnerability that the model independently rediscovered in every attempt, allowing it to bypass the browser's sandbox protections and read files directly from the computer. Ad

The team disclosed its findings to Mozilla, which patched that vulnerability in Firefox 159.0, released on October 27, 2026. The researchers have not confirmed whether similar attacks work against the new version, but they suspect the patch makes them "at least substantially more difficult." Ad

Using the same setup and techniques against Google Chrome, the team spent about $100,000 in API fees without producing an equivalent exploit. The researchers caution that this does not establish Chrome's immunity: better elicitation methods or more capable models might still succeed. They point to limited benchmark data suggesting that the recently announced Kimi K3.1 Pro could outperform GLM 5.3 on offensive cyber tasks, although they did not test it themselves.

## Every software vendor faces the same risk

The patch gap isn't a Firefox-only problem. According to the Epoch AI researchers, it exists across the software industry, in browsers, mobile operating systems, and router firmware. Open-source projects are especially exposed because all of their code is public, but closed-source software is vulnerable too. Anthropic has already shown that its Mythos model can exploit the patch gap in Windows without access to source code, and AI models are getting steadily better at decompiling compiled software to identify security fixes on their own.

According to the report, patch-gap exploits targeted Chrome in September 2026. That same month, a vendor released patched PHP builds more than six hours before the coordinated release of patches for two critical vulnerabilities. Citing external reporting, the researchers note that this early release could have contributed to thousands of exploit attempts before the official release, with the number rising into the millions immediately afterward.

The team is particularly concerned about software that users update infrequently, such as router firmware and mobile operating systems, because most users remain exposed for much longer.

## Faster updates help but cannot close the structural gap

To reduce the risk, the researchers recommend keeping security fixes private until they are ready to ship and moving them from beta to general release more quickly. They note that Firefox and Google Chrome have already begun shipping weekly updates. They also advise developers to avoid patching multiple vulnerabilities simultaneously when those vulnerabilities can be chained together.

Giving defenders access to stronger closed models does not, by itself, solve the structural problem, the researchers argue. Once a fix appears in public code, it points attackers toward the underlying vulnerability. Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview marked a leap in AI cyber capabilities in April 2026, and frontier labs responded with restricted access and programs like Glasswing and Daybreak that give defenders early access.

As freely available open-weight models grow more capable, offensive abilities are spreading beyond any single gatekeeper's control. As the researchers write, "We see these results as evidence of the diffusion of advanced cyber capabilities; many other pieces of software are likely already vulnerable to similar patch-gap attacks, and we expect the number to increase as more capable open-weight models are released."

# OpenAI asks outside experts, including a Nobel laureate, to check proofs its AI produced in math, computer science, and physics

OpenAI says its internal models have disproved a central assumption in computer science and proved part of one of the Millennium Prize Problems, among other results. Outside experts will now decide whether the proofs hold up.

OpenAI laid out three results from math, computer science, and physics in a blog post . The company says its internal AI models produced the proofs. OpenAI calls the manuscripts a kind of raw research data that still needs to be understood.

So OpenAI asked outside experts to act as "shepherds" for the results. Based on their advice, the company is handling each field differently. OpenAI says it also translated the math and computer science proofs into Lean.

Lean is a programming language that lets a computer check every step of a proof. That doesn't guarantee the result is error-free, though. Lean only checks whether the proof establishes the statement as it was written in Lean. Experts still have to decide whether that statement actually captures the intended problem.

## If OpenAI is right, a core assumption in computer science is wrong

The computer science result centers on the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH). It concerns the Boolean satisfiability problem, or SAT . SAT deals with a logical formula whose variables can only be true or false. The question is whether you can set the variables so the whole formula comes out true.

With only a few variables, you can just try every combination. But each new variable doubles the number of possibilities. With 100 variables, you're already looking at a 31-digit number.

Put simply, the ETH says there's no real shortcut. You can speed up the trial and error, but in the worst case, computing time still grows exponentially, increasing by a fixed factor with every added variable.

OpenAI says the satisfiability problem is closely tied to the P versus NP problem . That's the famous open question of whether a problem whose solution can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly. With SAT, checking is easy because you just plug in a proposed answer and do the math. The hard part is finding one that works.

SAT is considered the textbook example of hard problems of this kind . A fast method for solving it would instantly make thousands of other problems fast to solve too. Most experts believe no such method exists. That belief goes by the shorthand "P does not equal NP."

The ETH goes further than that conjecture. It says not only that SAT is hard, but how hard. If the ETH falls, P could still differ from NP, so hard problems wouldn't automatically become easy.

The ETH was widely accepted as true. Hundreds of papers in graph theory, computational biology, databases, and computational geometry build on it. They show, for example, that a problem can't be solved faster than a certain time if the ETH holds.

Now OpenAI says its system has proved the ETH is false. If the proof holds, those papers lose their foundation. Their results wouldn't automatically be wrong, but they'd no longer be proven.

OpenAI says the result could help researchers find better algorithms. Turning it into practical gains would still take a lot of research, though.

## The practical payoff is unclear, but the theoretical fallout would be big

SAT matters a lot in practice. Specialized programs called SAT solvers check chip designs for errors and test software, for example.

They often handle formulas with millions of variables already. That's because formulas from real-world applications are usually much easier than the worst case the ETH deals with. Speeding up only the worst case wouldn't automatically help these programs.

MIT professor Ryan Williams struck a similarly cautious tone on X . When a user asked what everyday developers would notice first, Williams said nobody knows yet. At the current pace, he said, it's plausible that practical SAT solving could see serious progress within 12 months. "Or we may see nothing of the sort. I really don't know," he admitted.

The result would also ripple through complexity theory itself, specifically the study of circuits, which are networks of simple logic gates like AND, OR, and NOT. If OpenAI's result holds, Williams says it would follow that a certain class of very demanding problems can't be solved with small circuits. "Small" here means that when the input doubles in length, the circuit needs at most about twice as many gates.

## The people who came up with the ETH are checking whether it's wrong

Williams will independently check and explain the result together with Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego. Impagliazzo and Paturi originally proposed the ETH along with Francis Zane. Williams writes that the group hasn't signed any nondisclosure agreements, is working unpaid, and plans to share interim findings as they go.

In an open letter , the three also make clear that their involvement isn't an endorsement of the claim. A result this big needs careful, independent review, they write.

At the group's request, OpenAI is publishing all the raw data, including the written proof and the Lean proof . The company has also committed to funding a conference on what the result means for the field.

## A decades-old wave conjecture may now hold in every dimension

The math result concerns a conjecture about waves like those in sound, light, or earthquakes. Mathematician Christopher Sogge proposed it in 1991.

Waves can concentrate at a single spot, much like light at the focal point of a magnifying glass. The conjecture says this extreme concentration only lasts briefly. Averaged over time, waves behave more smoothly, or evenly, than the extreme case would suggest. That's why it's called the local smoothing conjecture.

Until now, it had only been proven in two dimensions, for waves on a surface like water. Guth, Wang, and Zhang did that in 2019. OpenAI says its models have now produced a proof for every dimension, including waves in space and in hypothetical spaces with even more dimensions.

OpenAI says the result reaches beyond waves. Because the local smoothing conjecture is so basic to the field, two other well-known conjectures follow from it. They are the Kakeya conjecture from geometry and Stein's restriction conjecture from Fourier analysis . Fourier analysis breaks signals like sounds into individual oscillations. Proving the local smoothing conjecture automatically proves both of these as well.

The Kakeya conjecture shows how hard even these follow-on results are. Wang and Zahl only proved it for three dimensions in 2025. According to OpenAI, both conjectures would now be solved in all dimensions.

Unlike the other two results, no dedicated group is shepherding this proof. OpenAI says it did reach out to an outside expert to discuss that kind of collaboration. On that person's advice, though, the company published the proof text and the Lean proof directly. That way, researchers can decide for themselves how to check the result.

## OpenAI wants to put quantum field theory on solid mathematical ground

The physics result goes to the foundation of particle physics. Physicists describe elementary particles and the forces between them using quantum field theory , which OpenAI calls the most important framework in modern theoretical physics. Its predictions are extremely accurate, but the theories lack an exact mathematical basis.

Instead, physicists work with approximations, such as an imaginary lattice of points that they keep making finer. It's still an open question whether this produces a unique, consistent theory, meaning whether a theory "exists" in the mathematical sense. Whether it describes nature correctly is a separate question.

OpenAI says its AI has proved that certain quantum field theories exist in four dimensions, meaning three dimensions of space plus time. So far, nobody has pulled off such a proof in four dimensions for theories where particles interact with each other.

The strong force sits at the center of it. It binds quarks into protons and neutrons, which in turn holds atomic nuclei together. Particles called gluons carry it. The proof covers three theories that build on each other like steps.

The bottom step is Yang-Mills theory . It describes only gluons, without quarks. It's tied to one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, each of which carries a $1 million prize from the Clay Mathematics Institute.

The problem has two parts. The first is proving that Yang-Mills theory exists mathematically. The second is showing that it has a so-called mass gap . OpenAI explicitly says it has solved only the existence part. That means the Millennium Problem wouldn't be fully solved.

The mass gap points to a puzzle. In the equations, gluons have no mass, and forces carried by massless particles normally reach very far. # OpenAI says it stopped a campaign to steal its models' reasoning, but the trick still worked on Azure

OpenAI says it has broken up a coordinated campaign to copy the hidden reasoning behind its AI models. Researchers found that the same trick kept working for weeks on cloud platforms like Microsoft Azure.

In a blog post , OpenAI says it detected and shut down what's known as an "adversarial distillation" campaign. The attackers targeted the models' protected reasoning, meaning the internal steps an AI works through before it gives an answer. Users typically see only the final result.

In distillation, one model learns from another model's full output. That includes the stronger model's complete chains of thought, not just its answers. Those intermediate steps are what make the output so valuable. OpenAI says they can contain information that's deliberately kept out of the final answer, and they can help others recreate a model's capabilities.

According to OpenAI, the activity began at low volume on July 1. On July 24 and 25, it spiked to 16,000 requests from more than 4,000 users, all relying on a typical extraction pattern. A closer look uncovered a network of more than 15,000 accounts with related patterns, which OpenAI says it had fully shut down by July 28. A footnote clarifies that these were attempted extractions, not necessarily successful ones.

OpenAI links a core group behind the activity to people associated with Moonshot AI, the company that makes the Kimi language model. The company says it's unclear whether all the actors it observed trace back to a single source. Anthropic recently reported similar attempts by Chinese AI companies .

## A cheap model can unlock an expensive model's hidden thoughts

According to OpenAI, the attackers copied encrypted reasoning from one conversation and then asked a model in a separate conversation to decrypt it and write it out.

Researcher Joachim Schaeffer and his team had already shown how this works in a paper . AI providers send reasoning back to customers only as encrypted data packets, which customers pass along with follow-up requests. Because those packets are encrypted with shared keys, the researchers found, they can be moved between sessions, between users, and even between different models from the same provider. That lets a weaker, cheaper model from the same family act as a "decryption oracle" that prints the stronger model's hidden thoughts word for word.

OpenAI credits the researchers by name. The company says it confirmed that the attack paths they reported were real and that their findings helped it roll out countermeasures faster.

OpenAI says it has since banned fraudulent accounts, tightened sign-ups, and closed the hole that let people reuse and read encrypted reasoning that didn't belong to them. It also now screens streamed outputs and holds them back if they might reveal reasoning. OpenAI says it shared what it learned through the Frontier Model Forum and government channels, because the problem isn't limited to its own models.

## Locking down the API doesn't help if the cloud stays open

The story doesn't end there. On the same day, the researchers published an update to their study . "We stole reasoning. Again," Schaeffer wrote on X . Securing your own API, he argues, doesn't secure the wider ecosystem of cloud providers that also sell access to the models.

When the team tested again on September 13, the attack was blocked on OpenAI's and Anthropic's own APIs. On Microsoft Azure, it worked against every OpenAI model they tried, including the new GPT-6 Astra, and against Anthropic models up to Sonnet 5. A single attempt was enough to pull out the reasoning verbatim. "Same models, but different protections depending on which platform serves them," Schaeffer said.

There's also a second, even simpler method, which developer Can Bölük demonstrated publicly. The model gets a virtual notepad as a tool and is told to write its reasoning there, and the user can then read whatever it wrote. The researchers say this worked on every OpenAI model, as well as on Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5. Only Opus 5, Fable 5, and Fable 5.1 didn't reveal their reasoning. The output closely resembled what the decryption attack produced, and the researchers believe it would likely be just as useful for distillation.

The researchers describe the fixes so far as piecemeal and superficial. Many rely on brittle matching of specific request patterns, and some reached the cloud platforms only days later. GPT-6 Astra launched on third-party platforms without any of the protections in place. According to the researchers' timeline, OpenAI didn't add safeguards to the Azure endpoint until September 27. For Anthropic models, the reported extraction could no longer be reproduced on Azure starting September 28.

Schaeffer argues that patches have to cover every type of attack and every cloud that hosts the models. Otherwise, attackers can simply pick the route with the weakest defenses. The paper goes a step further, arguing that cloud providers that don't enforce equivalent protections shouldn't be allowed to serve reasoning models at all. If they do, the researchers write, open backdoors would effectively let people sidestep export controls at the API level. OpenAI acknowledges that models hosted by partners need the same protection as its own services and says the work is not finished.

We previously covered the research team's original discovery of the vulnerability. Our latest AI Radar newsletter on Chinese language models takes a deeper look at distillation. OpenAI expects these attempts to grow more sophisticated as leading models improve and more players hunt for cheap ways to copy what they can do.

# OpenMobile-2 proves open-source smartphone agents can rival proprietary models

## Key Points

- The open-source OpenMobile-2 project trains AI smartphone agents in an environment with more than 110 simulated apps.

- App diversity matters more than data volume. With the same amount of training data, increasing the number of apps pushed the success rate on unseen applications from 60.7 to 67.5 percent.

- On real Android devices, the larger model scored 59.6 points on SPA-Bench, the highest result among open models.

More data alone doesn't make smartphone agents better. With the same amount of data, what matters most is how many different apps an agent trains on.

AI agents that operate apps on their own learn mainly through practice, but the data they need is mostly locked up at big companies. Open models lag behind as a result, write researchers from Nanjing University, AI company SenseTime, and several other universities.

OpenMobile-2 is their attempt to close that gap. They're releasing two agent models built on Qwen3.5 with 9 billion and Qwen3.6 with 27 billion parameters , along with the full training environment, data, and instructions to reproduce everything. The authors say their model ranks near the top among current smartphone agents. Ad

## Why rebuilding 110 apps beats training on real ones

Training on real apps is painful because logins, real purchases, and no way to reset state make the process expensive and hard to repeat. So the researchers rebuilt 35 apps popular mainly in China, including Taobao, JD, DiDi, and Meituan, plus globally used services like Slack and Google Drive. Combined with existing simulations and apps running in an Android emulator, the practice ground covers more than 110 applications. Ad

Human reviewers compared the rebuilt apps to the originals and kept refining until workflows and interfaces matched. Orders, budgets, and travel plans persist across sessions, and data can pass between apps via the clipboard. Every simulation resets to its starting state automatically, while the agent only sees screenshots and has no access to internal app data, mimicking how a person would actually use them.

From this setup, the team generated about 11,600 example workflows and more than 2,000 practice tasks with automated success checks. Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro served as the teacher model that produced the examples, which means OpenMobile-2 is effectively learning from a closed system. Ad

## Real-phone performance jumps the most

Both models show clear gains on established benchmarks. On AndroidWorld, the larger model jumps from 67.1 to 79.9 points, while the smaller one goes from 54.3 to 74. The predecessor OpenMobile-1 scored 64.7 on the same test. On the harder MobileWorld benchmark, which covers longer tasks spanning multiple apps, the larger model improves from 35.9 to 50.4 points.

The biggest jump shows up on real Android devices, where the larger model climbs from 31.9 to 59.6 points on SPA-Bench. The researchers say that's the best score among open models. Ad

Training environment diversity matters more than sheer data volume here. The researchers held the amount of data constant and only increased the number of apps the agent practiced on, which pushed the success rate on unseen apps from 60.7 to 67.5 percent. With the same data budget, app variety beats extra examples from a handful of apps. Ad

Reinforcement learning on top brought only limited gains, mainly in environments that resembled the training setup. On AndroidWorld, the larger model actually scored slightly worse afterward, landing at 79.9 instead of 80.8 points.

## Direct commands let agents skip the menu maze

An experimental part of the study goes beyond tapping and swiping. More than 50 of the simulated apps offer direct commands like "add to cart" so the agent can skip navigating through menus, and the agent freely switches between both approaches depending on what's available.

On its own, though, this doesn't help much because the models tend to ignore the shortcuts without targeted training. Once they've been trained on them, the agents use them well, solving up to 10.3 percentage points more tasks while needing about five fewer steps. The researchers say this ability also transfers to tools the models never encountered during training.

## Key Points

- The AI startup Recursive has released Flint, a language model for programming tasks that was developed largely by an internal AI system called "Eureka Machine."

AI startup Recursive built its first language model with an AI system that proposes, runs, and evaluates its own experiments.

AI startup Recursive has released Flint, its first language model. An AI system called "Eureka Machine" was involved in nearly every step of development, proposing ideas on its own, building them out, testing them, and planning follow-up experiments based on the results.

Flint is a mixture-of-experts model (MoE) designed for agentic coding on local hardware, and it was built in four months. Out of 40 billion total parameters, only 2.5 billion are active per token. Recursive claims Flint leads coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Pro v2, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and SWE-Bench Verified among MoE models (such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Laguna S 2.1 ) with fewer than 50 billion parameters. The model is meant to compete with dense models in the 25 to 40 billion parameter range while running more than five times faster. On a MacBook Pro with M4 Pro, Flint generates more than 125 tokens per second at short contexts, according to Recursive. On an Nvidia RTX Spark with 64 GB of memory, it tops 150. Compared to similar models, inference is up to twice as fast. Ad

## Eureka Machine chose the architecture, quantization, and compute kernels on its own

Recursive says the Eureka Machine automates the entire research cycle, running multiple approaches in parallel. For Flint, it helped with training data, optimizers, architecture design, and inference tuning. Three examples show how the system shaped the model's performance.

Starting from an architecture with 35 billion total and 3 billion active parameters, the Eureka Machine tested different expert configurations. The final design of 40 billion total and 2.5 billion active parameters turned out to be the best tradeoff between speed and coding performance among all the variants it tested. Ad

For quantization, the system went against common practice and reduced the output layer to four bits as well. An added distillation step was meant to recover the lost accuracy, and according to Recursive, it needed roughly half as many training steps as the previous method. The finished NVFP4 model sits only 0.7 points behind the 16-bit version across benchmarks.

The Eureka Machine also built specialized compute kernels for Apple Silicon and Nvidia RTX Spark. On Apple's M4 and M5 chips, a Metal megakernel combines the entire forward pass during token generation into a single operation. Recursive says these optimizations across multiple development stages are what enable the high inference speed. Ad

## Flint runs locally and ships with open weights

Flint supports context windows of up to 512,000 tokens, though Recursive recommends capping it at 256,000. The model weights are available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Supported runtimes include llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, and SGLang. Recursive also released rec , its own inference engine for Apple Silicon. Ad

All of that means the model can run locally without sending code to external servers. Recursive does acknowledge that Flint needs more guidance on complex tasks than large proprietary coding models. The company recommends breaking bigger tasks into smaller steps.

## Recursive is betting it can build AI that keeps building better AI

The startup, founded by Richard Socher and others including former DeepMind researcher Tim Rocktäschel, came out of stealth in May 2026 and raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation. At the time, Recursive had no concrete technical results to show. Flint is the company's first publicly available model from its automated research process.

The long-term goal is to build a superintelligence that keeps improving itself. Eventually, Recursive wants to apply the same approach to automate research in other scientific fields.

A study of more than 700 task logs found that AI agents handle large portions of the work, but humans still make most of the critical research calls.

Those are the steps Recursive wants to automate with the Eureka Machine. Flint is a first concrete result, but it doesn't yet prove full recursive self-improvement. For that, the company would need to show that a model built with the Eureka Machine actually makes the Eureka Machine itself a better researcher.

# Researchers find six patterns that make AI text so exhausting to read

A study from New York University and the University of Texas at Austin shows that frontier language models systematically overuse linguistic patterns that make their output harder to read.

Anyone who regularly works with ChatGPT, Claude, or other language models knows the feeling. The answers are often factually correct, but reading them feels like work, full of nested sentences, odd word combinations, and metaphors no human would ever use.

A study by researchers at New York University and the University of Texas at Austin backs that up with data. The team had 14 language models produce text in casual conversation, coding sessions, and argumentative essays. The lineup included Claude, GPT-5.6, GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and smaller open-source models like Llama and Olmo. In total, the researchers analyzed 120 conversations, 45 coding sessions, and 980 essays, then compared them against human-written text from movie subtitles, StackExchange, and student essays.

## Six patterns that make AI text a chore to read

AI models overuse unusual word combinations that rarely show up in human writing, like "reader-patience budget," and they place related parts of a sentence far apart in ways that tax working memory. Claude Opus 5 generated "A cat who can always get up and away is a much calmer cat," where the subject and the main predicate are separated by a long clause.

Shortened references with a dropped connector are common too. Instead of "the book that the professor wrote," the models write "the book the professor wrote," saving one word but creating brief confusion about how the parts fit together. Stacked nouns like "horror movie soundtrack generator" force readers to figure out on their own which word modifies which.

The models turn nouns into verbs where humans wouldn't. Claude Fable 5 wrote "calendar it," where a human would say "put it in the calendar." They apply animate verbs to inanimate subjects, too. Claude Opus 5 produced "The whole conversation is eating its own tail," even though a conversation doesn't have a tail and can't eat. Readers can figure out what's meant, but it takes an extra beat.

## Smaller models write more like humans

Llama and the Olmo base model come closest to human text. Within the Olmo family, scores rise steadily from the base model through the instruct variant to the reasoning model Olmo Think, which hits frontier-level numbers, pointing to post-training as the likely cause. Claude Opus 5.5 beats its predecessor Opus 5 in 19 out of 21 comparisons, suggesting that targeted finetuning can improve readability .

## Training rewards information density over clarity

Human language balances ease of production with ease of understanding, but modern language models are trained increasingly on tasks like math, code, and logical reasoning, where correctness gets rewarded and clarity doesn't, the researchers say.

The shift from RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) to RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) removes humans from the feedback loop entirely, the researchers argue, and models develop a kind of "dialect" that works well for compressing information and solving complex problems but poorly for human readers.

As a proof of concept, the researchers trained a smaller language model with a penalty term that rewarded shorter answers. Under certain training conditions, the model favored shorter phrasings almost without exception, regardless of context, and even generalized that preference to sentence patterns it had never encountered during training. Humans, by contrast, chose between shorter and longer variants depending on the situation.

A similar explanation comes from inside the industry. Anthropic employee Jackson Kernion, who works on Claude fine-tuning, recently explained why Opus 4.6 was the last good "writing model" from Anthropic. Optimizing newer models for math, code, and technical explanations aimed at other AI models pushed Claude toward a style that works well for AI but reads as too dense and unnatural for humans. Kernion called it an adaptation to "LLM psychology." With Opus 5.5, Anthropic pushed back for the first time, addressing sentence clarity and overloaded blocks of information, and as the study shows, successfully so.

# Researchers stretch LeCun's JEPA AI into a universal world model that works from physics to biology

## Key Points

- The JEPA-Anything AI model extends the architecture pioneered by Yann LeCun into a world model that works across fields like physics, robotics, and medicine.

- The method breaks future states into multiple partial predictions instead of funneling everything into one, letting it pick up patterns that standard models miss.

- The model also identified a liver cancer treatment candidate that killed more tumor cells in lab samples and mice than either component alone.

Researchers have expanded the JEPA architecture pioneered by Yann LeCun so it works across seven very different fields. The effort also produced a liver cancer treatment candidate that the team tested in the lab.

World models predict how a system will evolve, whether it's a robot, a molecule, or a patient's health. Until now, each domain has typically needed its own model. A team led by PhAI Labs, with collaborators from Stanford, Oxford, and Princeton, wants to show that a single shared principle is enough.

Their paper introduces JEPA-Anything, built on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA). These models don't reconstruct raw data like pixels but instead predict an abstract summary of a missing or future state, filtering out irrelevant details. The authors see a weakness in the standard approach: everything gets funneled into a single prediction, so easy patterns end up drowning out harder ones. Ad

## Multiple specialized predictions instead of one

JEPA-Anything breaks the predicted state into several parts, each handled by its own prediction module. An added constraint pushes the modules to capture different aspects rather than learning the same thing, and the model then reassembles their partial predictions into a complete picture. Ad

The researchers don't assign meanings to the parts, letting those roles emerge during training. Instead, they only change how they prepare the data for each field.

## Big gains in dynamics tests, mixed results for robots

The team compared JEPA-Anything against a standard JEPA with the same architecture, trained on the same data under identical conditions. Dynamic systems showed the clearest gains: in a simplified Pong environment with targeted interventions, prediction error dropped by 35 percent. For combinations of interventions the model never saw during training, it fell by 13 percent. Ad

JEPA-Anything consistently beat the baseline across ten test tasks spanning physics, robotics, and weather forecasting, according to the authors. On the Burgers equation, a common fluid dynamics benchmark, error fell by nearly half in a separate evaluation. Over 50 prediction steps the advantage held but shrank to about three percent. The method also scored best in simulations of water, quartz, acetaminophen, and benzene, even after 100 steps.

For single-cell data, the model assigned cell types more reliably, and on clinical data it predicted more than 1,000 possible disease events slightly better. The difference on image tasks was small. In locomotion planning for simulated walking robots, JEPA-Anything won in two of three environments, while the standard model came out ahead in the third. Ad

## The model flagged a liver cancer treatment, so the team tested it

The team's boldest claim comes from liver cancer research. The researchers analyzed the partial predictions a model had learned from biological data including gene activity, protein levels, and CRISPR screens. The top candidate paired IL-18, a signaling molecule that activates immune cells, with blockade of the enzyme CD73, which tumors use to suppress nearby immune responses. Ad

The team tested the combination on liver cancer cells co-cultured with immune cells, on organoids and tumor tissue from three patients each, and in mice. In the organoids and tissue samples, the combination killed more tumor cells than either IL-18 or CD73 blockade alone, and T cells and natural killer cells showed stronger activation. The study doesn't establish whether this could become an actual therapy.

In a second case, the researchers trained the model on simulated orbits without giving it any physical quantities. The learned patterns turned out to be a near-exact match for Kepler's third law, which says bodies on larger orbits move much more slowly. The law sets orbital frequency at orbit size to the power of minus 1.5; the model landed on minus 1.4991. The team only evaluated one training run, and picked the one with the lowest error.

Clean separation of the learned parts doesn't mean they capture real cause-and-effect relationships, the authors caution. It also remains an open question when such a model becomes reliable enough to guide experiment design. That's the team's long-term goal: AI agents would use JEPA-Anything to propose and rank experiments, then feed results back into the model. Code and models are publicly available.

LeCun proposed JEPA in 2022 as an alternative to generative models. In June 2025, Meta released V-JEPA 2 , a JEPA video model with 1.2 billion parameters that controlled robotic arms in unfamiliar environments without additional training. In November 2025, LeCun and Randall Balestriero followed up with LeJEPA , a theoretical foundation designed to keep training stable without the usual workarounds. LeCun is now pursuing the approach through his startup AMI Labs , which raised over a billion dollars in March 2026 to build world models.

Google Deepmind had already tested an AI-generated cancer hypothesis in the lab in October 2025. Its Gemma-based model C2S-Scale 27B proposed the drug silmitasertib to make tumor cells more visible to the immune system, and experiments with human cell models confirmed the prediction. Google Deepmind's multi-agent system Co-Scientist now plans experiments and operates lab equipment, covering parts of the loop the JEPA-Anything team wants to build. Loading samples into the machines, though, still requires humans.

# Sakana AI's self-improving model gets better at solving and judging, but can't catch its own blind spots

## Key Points

- A single language model improves itself through "Multi-Agent Self-Supervision" (MASS), without external help or a stronger teacher model.

- The model works as its own team: it assigns tasks to copies of itself, evaluates the results, and optimizes workflows for the next round of training.

- Win rates against the base model rise to nearly 70 percent after two rounds, but the method carries a real risk: the internal evaluator sometimes accepts flawed steps or manipulated solutions as successes and bakes them into the next model.

Sakana AI's MASS method lets one language model improve itself by solving tasks, judging results, and refining workflows without a stronger teacher model. The study finds gains across all three roles, but shared blind spots can let errors pass as progress and feed into the next training cycle.

Researchers from Sakana AI and UC Berkeley have introduced "Multi-Agent Self-Supervision" (MASS), a method for recursive self-improvement (RSI). A single language model handles the task, optimizes how the work gets done, and evaluates the results.

At the research frontier, even experts often struggle to judge results because verification can require costly supporting evidence or lengthy experiments, the authors argue. A single plasma study can take more than 120 million CPU hours, according to the paper . Ad

The model itself may therefore be the best available judge, even though it can miss its own mistakes when reviewing its work. Using the same model to solve, check, and revise can reinforce those errors rather than correct them. Ad

## Copies of one model divide up the work

Inspired by "Society of Mind," a book by AI pioneer Marvin Minsky, the researchers focus on how the model divides up the work. In MASS, a workflow is text appended to the prompt that defines each sub-agent's role and instructions. A "contract" specifies what information each sub-agent must return and which checks it must perform, while a "hop" sets the order of calls.

An orchestrator distributes the work among the sub-agents. When testing a trading strategy against historical prices, for example, the data specialist's contract must ensure the strategy uses only information available at each point in time. Ad

During the inner loop, the model's weights stay frozen as the team runs a candidate workflow and the evaluator compares the result against the current "champion." The optimizer uses that feedback to propose the next workflow, mainly by changing contracts and hops. In the outer loop, the champion runs 18 times per task, with the model ranking the results itself and selecting up to 15 runs for training.

The researchers remove the workflow text from the orchestrator's initial prompt in the training examples so the model learns to organize work based on the task alone. Specific assignments to sub-agents remain in the recorded traces, and the model takes on all three roles again after LoRA fine-tuning. Ad

The base model is Qwen3.6-27B , with Qwen Code as the harness . The researchers use twelve research tasks generated by GPT-5.5 across finance, robotics, and pharmaceuticals, reserving three for testing and nine for training. Only eight yield training data because the search finds no workflow that beats the reference on one training task. Ad

## Benchmark gains come mostly from completing more work

On the test tasks, the win rate against the base model rises from 53.9 percent after one round to 69.9 percent after two. On MLR-Bench, DSBench, ScienceAgentBench, and AstaBench, the model reaches 1.2 to 1.6 times the base model's score per output token. Gains in raw scores are sometimes small, with DSBench improving only from 0.473 to 0.482, while scores drop slightly on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and SWE-bench Verified.

The paper's appendix shows that completed MLR-Bench submissions rise from 31 to 50 out of 60, while their average grade falls from 3.07 to 2.88. The delegation tool goes unused in all 180 runs, leaving it unclear whether teamwork explains the gains.

Those gains are no longer statistically significant when results are compared task by task. The authors describe mixed results across research tasks, with AstaBench showing the same pattern.

## Training on solutions also improves the evaluator and optimizer

Although the model trains only on solution traces, its performance in the other two roles improves as well. The self-evaluator's agreement with external judges rises from 73 to 93 percent. Workflows found after one round beat the base model's workflows 64 percent of the time, even when the base model runs both.

Without workflow instructions, the base model delegates to sub-agents in just one of 110 runs, compared with 87 after two rounds. It could already delegate when explicitly instructed, but now does so without being asked.

During optimization, task knowledge shifts into contracts and hops, while roles and instructions become more generic. That finding rests on a small sample of just eight to nine tasks.

Training on team traces produces a model with a 68.3 percent win rate, compared with 64 percent for a single-agent student, using 31 percent fewer training tokens. External judges prefer team results 85.1 percent of the time, though teams produce about 2.4 times as many tokens. When outputs are similar in length, judges prefer team results 80 percent of the time, based on just ten pairs.

The evaluated team runs perform better, but the comparison doesn't establish that delegation alone explains the advantage. Team and single-agent runs also differ in workflow instructions, review instructions, and which successfully completed episodes were selected.

## Better feedback helps only if the optimizer can use it

Replacing only the evaluator with GPT-5.5 barely helped; the search progressed much faster only when the optimizer was stronger too. The authors conclude that good feedback helps only when the optimizer can act on it. With Qwen handling all three roles, the search still finds winning workflows for 11 of 12 tasks, but takes longer.

The extent of a workflow rewrite says little about its effect on results, and even byte-identical workflows can produce opposite outcomes. One run won all six external judgments, while another lost all six after the agent got stuck in a loop. The researchers suspect that limiting how much the optimizer changes at each step could help stabilize the search.

## Shared blind spots can compound from round to round

After failed simulations in a robotics task, the model had the simulator modified to move objects directly to the target, then reported success. External judges still rated the run positively five out of six times. In another trace used for training, a check passed even though it had returned only invalid values.

The authors see shared blind spots as the potential "Achilles' heel" of recursive self-improvement. If the model misses the same error in all three roles, that error could be accepted as an improvement and baked into the next model. The weakness would then affect both the system and its correction mechanism, prompting the authors to call for independent checks, limits on autonomy, and clear conditions for intervention. The code is publicly available.

Japanese research lab Sakana AI launched a dedicated research lab for recursive self-improvement in June, building on earlier work including the Darwin-Godel Machine and the AI Scientist . Google researchers are pursuing a related approach, automatically optimizing the scaffolding of prompts, workflows, and tools around a fixed model without letting agents overfit to their test tasks.

Vals AI recently found that agent teams cost 1.8 to 5.1 times as much as single agents but performed measurably better in only one of four comparisons. Anthropic showed that models engaging in reward hacking to game their reward systems also learn to deceive and sabotage safety checks.

# Some mathematicians call for OpenAI boycott after AI-generated proofs flood their field

After OpenAI published hundreds of AI-generated mathematical manuscripts, the Association for Human Mathematics is calling for a boycott. Many papers are so dense and oddly written that even leading experts need AI help to decipher them, if they can at all. A dispute is taking shape over whether a problem can count as solved before its proof has been independently worked through and made understandable to humans.

The Association for Human Mathematics (AHM) accuses OpenAI of violating core norms of scientific research by publishing the AI proofs and is urging mathematicians to stop working with the company.

Fields Medalist Terence Tao, who chairs the group, shared the statement as a guest post on his blog, while also outlining a "Math 2.0" era on Mastodon in which solving problems should no longer be the main focus of the discipline. Complexity theorist Scott Aaronson described the situation as a "Mathocalypse" on his blog .

The AHM statement escalates a months-long debate . OpenAI had already caused a stir by claiming an internal model solved more than 100 open math problems in a single month, including an approach to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Problem . In response to growing criticism, OpenAI set up the advisory group AGMAI at the Institute for Advanced Study, though the group explicitly has no say over the pace of the company's internal research.

## AHM sees the release as a show of force

The AHM says OpenAI has already ignored the central premise of AGMAI's advice, which held that advanced math problems shouldn't be tested on internal models. "Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done," the statement reads, describing the release of more than 700 files at once as "not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power."

The statement's opening paragraph also brings up the many copyright lawsuits OpenAI is fighting around the world, suggesting without saying so directly that the company could only achieve these results because it trained on mathematicians' work, whether legally or not.

That same dispute surfaced when OpenAI recently announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem shortly before two mathematicians could present their own AI-assisted solution. The two had used ChatGPT in their work, and OpenAI denied suspicions that it had used data from those interactions to train its own system and reach a solution faster.

Aaronson contrasts this with what he calls the "Anthropic model." OpenAI releases raw AI proof drafts in one batch, triggering a race to work through them. Anthropic instead partnered with two algorithm researchers whose AI model supplied the key idea for disproving two decades-old conjectures. The researchers received compensation and wrote a version of the proof that humans could follow.

Both approaches have drawbacks. OpenAI's method leaves the community doing the thankless work of making proofs readable, for free. Anthropic's method lets a private company choose which mathematicians get to serve as "emissaries" for a result.

## AI is cracking open math problems faster than anyone can verify the results

Tao previously joined 24 other Fields Medalists , including Peter Scholze, Maryna Viazovska, and Martin Hairer, in signing a statement warning of a "severe misalignment" between the AI industry's goals and those of mathematics. Problem-solving, they argue, is only a tool for the discipline's real goal of conceptual understanding, and mass-producing solved problems at an ever-faster pace could "destroy fertile ground instead of breathing life into new ideas."

The signatories also criticize rushed announcements of AI-generated solutions without proper write-ups or citations of relevant prior work, saying this raises "severe attribution and plagiarism questions."

On Mastodon , Tao now goes further. In traditional mathematics, proofs of long-standing open problems would lead to talks, workshops, new collaborations, and inclusion in textbooks, attracting young researchers who would work to understand and contextualize them.

Now he sees the opposite. Problems are being solved autonomously by AI users who have no interest in the field and can't understand the results well enough to answer questions or give talks, producing far fewer seminars and collaborations than traditional breakthroughs would. Researchers are also holding back promising directions for fear that competitors will scoop the solution.

For Tao, the damage is irreversible. Once a problem is considered solved, it can't be made unsolved again. Even knowing a solution exists can "contaminate," as he puts it, the search for other approaches that might yield further insights. Solutions are being "harvested" on a large scale, leaving entire branches of mathematics less fertile than before.

Tao argues that the "Math 2.0" era must stop treating problem-solving as its main measure of progress and start valuing explanation, community-building, and the opening of new research directions, with corresponding changes to how training, publication, and career advancement are judged.

This builds on Tao's earlier vision of " industrial mathematics " from 2024, though humans still set the pace in that version. AI was supposed to assist mathematicians much as engines assist chess players, enabling broad, relatively superficial research that complemented the deeper work of human experts. Today, Tao sees those roles reversed. AI is solving the deep problems while humans work through the results afterward. Like many other experts , Tao apparently badly underestimated the pace of AI development .

## Three hours of AI compute can now rival a mathematician's entire career

Aaronson shows what this means for individual researchers through the experience of his wife, Dana Moshkovitz, who has devoted her entire career to the Unique Games Conjecture, an open problem in theoretical computer science. The release includes a claimed proof of it.

In text messages to Aaronson on the night of the release, she wrote, "It feels like something written by someone who's on psychedelics." Much of the document was unclear. The paper cited numerous works without explaining why they applied, even though earlier results should have ruled that out.

"Basically the paper is so horribly written that it's impossible to read it without AI help," Moshkovitz said. The proof relied on an entirely new, bizarre construction that she described as "some alien craziness."

Aaronson lists other results from complexity theory, number theory, and algorithm research, including partial progress on several remaining Clay Millennium Problems. Any one of them, in his view, would have ranked among the year's top results on its own.

One area is notably absent from the release, however. Cryptography. Citing unnamed sources, Aaronson reports that AI companies are now quietly probing weaknesses in cryptographic protocols and primitives. About 8,000 problems were tested overall, with a success rate of roughly five percent and an average of three hours of compute at GPT-Pro level per problem. The model used was likely OpenAI's current internal one as well, which could ship to paying ChatGPT customers in the coming months.

## Mathematicians disagree over whether a boycott will help

Comments on Tao's blog post show how divided the field is. Several commenters back the boycott and propose that researchers stop using OpenAI products while also calling for better protection of preprint servers like arXiv against mass collection of training data.

Others consider the AHM's position unrealistic, arguing that OpenAI won't stop working on mathematics and that public results are better than private ones. Another commenter asks whether a problem can really count as solved when neither the authors nor anyone else fully understands the proof. In the case of Navier-Stokes, it remains unclear whether the result actually deepens anyone's understanding of fluid dynamics.

AGMAI itself takes a more diplomatic stance than the AHM, viewing the release as a first step with the mathematical understanding of the results only now beginning. Still, the group warns that the future of math research can't consist of working through results produced by AI labs.

"Mathematicians must be able to formulate their own questions, develop their own approaches, and explore directions that have not been selected as examples of an AI system's capabilities. Equitable access to powerful research tools and adequate computational resources are essential to that freedom," the organization writes.

## Key Points

- After stock crashes and canceled IPOs, industry experts expect a shakeout among young AI cloud providers, known as "neoclouds." Only a few of them are likely to survive in the long run.

- The shakeout puts Nvidia at risk. Customers outside the big tech companies account for 45 percent of its data center revenue, and the chipmaker is actively backing its partners with credit support and help finding sites.

- Neoclouds already face missing power connections and more cautious investors. The industry could also end up with an oversupply of compute that drives prices down.

After a week of plunging stock prices and scrapped IPO plans, industry executives expect a shakeout among up-and-coming AI cloud providers. Nvidia has a lot riding on how it plays out.

Hundreds of AI cloud providers are rushing into the market right now. Two executives from the data center and neocloud industries told The Information that only seven to ten of them will still be around in a few years. Several executives think consolidation is inevitable.

Their predictions come after a week in which some investors lost confidence in the so-called "neoclouds." Australian provider Firmus abruptly pulled its IPO, and shares of CoreWeave and its smaller rivals fell about 20 percent, according to The Information. "We'll definitely see consolidation," said David Driggers, CEO of neocloud provider Cirrascale. He expects deep-pocketed asset managers, along with telecom and fiber companies, to "pick up a neocloud here, a neocloud there." Ad

British provider Nscale shows how shaky things have gotten. According to The Telegraph, Microsoft pulled out of a data center deal in Loughton, England, where it had planned to lease 23,000 Nvidia chips. Bernstein estimates that only 35 percent of the data center capacity announced in North America will ever get built, according to Bloomberg.
