# Two German courts now hold Google liable for what its AI overviews say

## Key Points

- In a preliminary injunction, the Aachen Regional Court barred Google from spreading false claims about a doctor through its AI search results. The system had attributed criminal allegations and proceedings to him that actually involved a different person.

- The court relied on a Munich Regional Court I ruling and classified the AI-generated texts not as mere links to third-party websites but as Google's own statements, making the company directly liable.

- Google dodged a binding higher-court ruling in the Munich case by settling, but courts keep applying the same reasoning. If this legal view holds up, the consequences for Google could reach far beyond individual false claims.

Google tried to overturn a landmark Munich ruling on liability for AI search summaries by appealing, then quietly settled. Now a second court has applied the same reasoning. Google's AI answers count as the company's own content, and Google is responsible for them.

In late May, the Munich Regional Court I ruled in a widely watched case that Google is directly liable for the content of its AI-generated search summaries. Google's AI had falsely linked two Munich-based publishers to fraud schemes. The judges classified AI Overviews not as mere search results but as Google's own statements, meaning the company itself has to answer for them.

Instead of hiding behind the role of a neutral middleman passing along third-party information, Google would have to own the unlawful statements its AI produces. For a search feature that constantly generates new answers, that's a legal risk that's hard to quantify. If this view holds up, it could call into question the entire business model of AI search in Germany and shape the debate in other countries too. Ad

The distinction between a search reference and original content could also have consequences beyond false factual claims. If AI answers count as Google's own content, the publishers whose texts Google uses to generate those answers might eventually assert their own claims. That wasn't part of the Munich case, but it's a logical next step. Ad

As THE DECODER has learned, the appeal Google publicly announced was never carried through to a decision. The case ended in a settlement instead, meaning no higher court ever weighed in on the Munich reasoning. Why the settlement was reached and whether money changed hands is unknown. Neither Google nor the affected publisher would comment. The court also declined to weigh in on the broader significance of its own ruling beyond this specific case.

## A settlement can't erase the Munich court's reasoning

The Munich judges' legal reasoning isn't dead, though. In a decision dated September 24, 2026, the Aachen Regional Court barred Google from spreading certain false statements and explicitly relied on the Munich ruling's reasoning. Google can challenge the injunction. The decision isn't final yet. Ad

In this new case, a physician in Aachen fought back against serious false claims in Google's "AI Mode" search feature. The doctor had worked as chief physician and professor of neuroradiology from 2010 until late June 2026. On August 28, a colleague alerted him that Google's AI was explaining his departure by citing an alleged sexual assault against his secretary. When users ran additional searches using terms like "suspension," "termination," and "court proceedings," AI Mode returned detailed, multi-paragraph fabrications. It even invented a complete legal aftermath.

None of the allegations or proceedings had anything to do with the doctor. The AI had taken events involving a different former university professor and pinned them on him, something the Aachen court could confirm from its own records since the criminal case had actually been brought against someone else. Cases of AI misattribution like this have been documented before . Ad

## Google refuses to delete the content and risks steep fines

Even though the doctor described the mix-up in detail in late August and asked Google by email to remove the content, the company said in mid-September that it would take no action. A formal legal demand sent the same day also went nowhere. Google confirmed receiving it, but according to the court, the false AI-generated texts were still live. Ad

The Aachen Regional Court then banned further spread of the three disputed text variants. Because the false claims could seriously damage the doctor's professional reputation, the court acted on an emergency basis without hearing Google first. If Google violates the order, it faces fines of up to 250,000 euros per violation.

The most significant part of the Aachen decision is how closely it tracks the Munich reasoning, suggesting a consistent legal view is forming across German courts. Google uses its AI to produce its own statements rather than simply making third-party information findable. "The respondent provides AI-generated search and is therefore also responsible for the answers generated in this context," the court wrote.

Aachen even cites the Munich ruling directly, noting that Google's AI produces "independent, new, and substantive statements based on an evaluation and combination of content from various third-party websites."

Google could check such statements, the court said, for example, by comparing AI output against the source websites it used. The Aachen judges added that had Google confronted its own AI with the doctor's objections, the system would have caught the errors itself.

## The stakes go far beyond individual false claims

Both cases raise the question of what long-term legal strategy Google is pursuing with its AI search features. If German courts keep classifying the company as a publisher of false statements and Google keeps dodging precedent through what are likely financial settlements, that creates a perverse incentive.

For specialized law firms and affected parties, it could turn into a lucrative business model. They could probe AI search with targeted queries until the language model stitches together false, potentially defamatory statements, then file for an injunction and negotiate a settlement. These systems are easy to manipulate.

Of course, Google can afford to make individual cases disappear this way for years, since binding precedent only happens when at least one side pushes the legal process all the way to the end. But Google's motivation likely goes well beyond liability for individual false claims. If a top court were to rule that AI answers count as original content, the publishers whose texts feed those answers could assert their own claims too. In the most extreme scenario, Google would have to compensate the creators behind its sources for every AI-generated answer. That would upend the economics of AI search entirely.

# With AI writing the code, entrepreneurial thinking is now what counts most for newcomers at Anthropic

Felix Rieseberg, an engineering manager at Anthropic, has scrapped the classic coding interview. He argues that AI makes the tests pointless and that ambitious young developers can use it to overtake more experienced colleagues.

Rieseberg, who has led development of Claude.ai and Claude Code Desktop at Anthropic, says there's no longer any reason to give candidates small programming tasks. Claude now handles them better than the candidates do, he says. In his view, handing someone a little React challenge makes as little sense today as quizzing them on Assembly.

On his teams, good test scores no longer predict who turns out to be a top developer. Instead, he's watching relatively new engineers overtake more experienced colleagues. "Hunger beats tenure," he says. Rieseberg aims his post at "junior" developers, though he deliberately redefines the term. He doesn't necessarily mean people just starting out. He means any engineer without social status, power, or a network inside their company.

## Why newcomers spot the problems veterans stopped seeing

Rieseberg argues that newcomers have a structural advantage because they notice problems that long-time employees accepted as givens years ago. He points to organizational researcher James March, who wrote in 1991 that organizations depend on a steady stream of naive and uninformed newcomers. Stripe founder Patrick Collison has also explicitly urged new hires to flag anything that seems strange to them. Veterans, he noted, stopped noticing those friction points long ago.

Rieseberg cites his time at Notion as an example. He was asked to design an offline architecture that people inside the company considered impossible. The data model was too complex, and CEO Ivan Zhao would supposedly never accept the only workable solution. The technical hurdle was real, but the founder's resistance wasn't. Nobody had asked him, because everyone treated it as common knowledge.

## Cheap execution weakens the old hierarchy

The core problem for newcomers, Rieseberg says, is that nobody in the company listens to them. Because execution used to be expensive, organizations were built so that a few decision-makers could approve or block ideas. You had to work your way up a rigid hierarchy before management trusted you to actually build something. AI changes that equation because execution is no longer expensive, Rieseberg writes.

His first piece of advice builds on a 2011 quote from Patrick McKenzie, who wrote that "engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things." Developers should understand what their company is really trying to achieve and attach themselves to the parts that make money. A useful starting point is knowing your manager's manager's goals.

From there, he suggests picking an ambitious idea that would dramatically advance those goals and building a working prototype over a weekend. That skips the usual cycle of product specs, approvals, and lobbying designers or product managers. The key is to focus on one good idea instead of hiding three good ones among 20 bad ones. Anyone who builds a prototype that includes a new programming language, a backend, and mobile apps all at once will fail. The prototype should get the idea across so clearly that leadership immediately sees both the opportunity and the right person to run with it.

## Newcomers have the edge on empathy

Rieseberg distinguishes between two types of engineers. Newcomers working on user-facing products bring a natural empathy for outside users. Long-tenured colleagues at Slack or Notion had a hard time seeing things from an outside user's perspective. Engineers working on infrastructure or internal tools, on the other hand, benefit from not knowing why something is supposed to be impossible.

He backs this up with an example from his own company. Two Anthropic engineers who were relatively new at the time, Anthony Morris and Alice Zhao, built the graphical interface for Claude Code over a weekend. The first public version shipped about eight days later.

Rieseberg now looks for small prototypes in job applications that show taste, empathy, and principled thinking. The classic coding interview isn't coming back, he says.

On one hand, Rieseberg's advice reads as a message of empowerment. AI becomes an equalizer that lets newcomers get past gatekeepers who've gone blind to their own company's problems. On the other hand, it moves the bar for entry-level jobs away from diligence and craft toward entrepreneurial thinking, product sense, and taste. Most universities barely teach those skills, and companies have traditionally expected them from experienced product managers or founders.

The engineers he holds up as models also build prototypes on weekends without being asked. "Hunger beats tenure" sounds motivating, but it assumes a hustle mentality that not every new developer can bring to the job.
